Mr. Speaker, the management of Canadian National Railways advise that in common with all large organizations it obtains from time to time technical advice or consultation on specific problems. The term "management consultant" is not susceptible to precise definition. However, in the general consulting field the firm of Woods Gordon and Company has been assisting the company in its general reorganization. What was the amount of reserves in the exchange fund on the close of business on (a) June 20, 1961, (b) June 30, 1961, (c) the latest available date?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This question asks what was the amount of reserves in the exchange fund on the close of business on (a) June 20, 1961, (b) June 30, 1961 and (c) at the latest available date.
As I have pointed out on earlier occasions, it has never been the practice to issue figures on the holdings of exchange except at the month end. These figures are published at the end of each month. They refer to the holdings of gold and foreign exchange, usually U.S. dollars, which are official holdings. Practically all of the official holdings are in the exchange fund. It is not the practice to issue the figures apart from the total. In total the official holdings, as I say, are nearly all in the exchange fund.
Now as to the holdings, in keeping with the practice I shall begin by giving the figure on May 31. It is not one of the dates that appear in this question, but in keeping with the practice observed at all times in the past I am coming as close as I can to the dates that are mentioned in the question. On May 31 the official holdings of gold and United States dollars at the close of business that day were $1,949.2 million. On June 30 they were $1,985.2 million. Mr. Speaker, the date June 20 happens to be the date of the budget, and is a date, not being a month end, when it has not been customary to issue any statement as to holdings. The same would apply to part (c) of the question, the latest available date. I think therefore, Mr. Speaker, I should not depart from the practice that has been observed, but I may perhaps suggest that there has been no significant or great change in the figures.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Answered.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Assiniboia asked me the following question:
In view of the fact that the new crop year is just a few weeks away, and the government has stated there would be a review of the policy of the wheat board in relation to the delivery of grain to feed mills, has any consideration been given to this policy-

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Acting Minister of Agriculture):
maintopic: STATEMENT ON DELIVERIES TO FEED MILLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in November, 1960 the Canadian wheat board announced a new policy in respect of deliveries by producers to feed mills, which was to remain in effect until the conclusion of the present crop year on July 31 next, at which time this policy would be subject to review by the board.
In the application by a feed mill for designation as a non-quota feed mill provision is made whereby the mill will supply periodically to the board information in respect of its purchases of wheat, oats and barley from permit holders. The final report from the mills must be submitted to the board on or before August 15, 1961. This information will form an integral part of the data to be considered by the board in the review of its feed mill policy and, as a consequence, this review cannot take place until subsequent to August 15, 1961.
In the interim it is the intention of the board to extend its present policy beyond the end of the current crop year until the review of its feed mill policy can be completed, which should be toward the latter part of August, 1961.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext:
I can locate it by saying to the hon. member that it was during the evening of the governor general's dinner.
Everybody in this house was under the impression at first that this matter had been discussed in plenary session during the talks and meetings that were held here in Ottawa between representatives of the federal and provincial governments.
Now, following the questions asked by the hon. member for Laurier, the minister told us that it was just an intimate conversation which took place during or after a dinner given by His Excellency the Governor General. That is not all, Mr. Speaker. We learned yesterday that the version which the Minister of Finance gave to the house is not true to the facts. His statement was most emphatically contradicted by the other interested party, the premier of the province of Quebec. Indeed, here is what he said in that connection:
I read in the newspapers, this morning, a Canadian Press report on a debate which occurred in the House of Commons yesterday concerning federal grants to universities.
It is reported in that dispatch that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) stated that I have asked him to leave out of the legislation "any reference" to the agreement signed in that regard, in 1960, with the Quebec provincial government.
I must say I have never made such a request to Mr. Fleming. There has been no communication between the Minister of Finance and myself, either orally or by letter.
The subject was discussed briefly in the course of a friendly and private conversation during a dinner given by His Excellency the Governor General, in February. We discussed together the proposals I made as early as in July 1960 concerning the federal government's gradual withdrawal

Income Tax Act
from the joint programs and the progressive return to the provinces of their taxation rights so that the latter may fully meet their obligations in that respect.
From one thing to the other, we got to speak about Bill C-56 which has become chapter 13 of the 1960 federal statutes. I have never asked or even suggested the abolition of the 1 per cent abatement granted corporations in the provinces which handle university grants themselves.
I just reiterated to Mr. Fleming some criticism I had, in any case, publicly voiced before, against one provision in Bill C-56. I am thinking of the clause allowing the federal government to deduct from equalization payments the surplus revenue which the additional taxation of 1 per cent yields to a province-which is the surplus amount received from the federal government by the universities under the federal act. I added that we should try to find something better to fully safeguard provincial autonomy. As far as I remember, the conversation on the subject did not go any further.
I repeat that I have not since received any communication from Mr. Fleming or from the Prime Minister and that I myself did not get in touch with the federal government or with any of its ministers or officials.
Needless to say that I was greatly surprised this morning at reading this item announcing onesided action by the federal government. There is certainly a misunderstanding somewhere. I fully trust that the federal government will be ready to start negotiations with us to settle the matter, said Mr. Lesage.
Mr. Speaker, this is not the first time during the last weeks that statements by the Minister of Finance have been denied. It would be useless to quote other instances of such incidents which are familiar to all. But this new incident is of very great significance and extremely serious, because it endangers good relations between the central government and the provincial governments, those relations being essential to the good operation of our administrative system.

Mr. Lesage admits that such conversations took place, although he does not place upon them the interpretation placed by the minister.
I remind hon. members that while no one can comment on what transpired at the in camera sessions, Mr. Lesage outside the in camera meetings did publicly discuss in complete and full detail the various features of the government's proposal. In fact one might say he dotted the i's and crossed the t's. I believe I am correct in saying that at no time did Mr. Lesage refer to the question of university grants within the framework of the government's proposal. If following that he was dissatisfied that this was not discussed within the framework of federal-provincial relations, if he felt it should have been in the government's proposal, or if he did not feel in accord with what was said by the Minister of Finance, certainly one might have expected some comment from him either at that time or since.
It is clear that this legislation will continue in force until March 31, 1962. There has been no indication on the part of the government that any other course would be followed. The Minister of Finance indicated his willingness to meet with authorities of the province of

Quebec to discuss this matter and make mutually suitable arrangements. The position of the minister has not changed since he made that statement. From the events that have transpired it is clear that there must have been some understanding that the matter was not to be discussed at the time of the conference.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: Hon. members who now protest that statement were not present at the conference. Certainly there was no comment indicating a possible change. It is clear that there is no difficulty concerning the effecting of a satisfactory arrangement between the federal government and the province of Quebec or between the federal government and any other province that wishes to adopt this course between the present time and the time at which the present arrangement concludes in March of 1962.

Mr. Speaker, I rise in an effort to clarify my position. In his opening remarks the hon. member for Edmonton West said that the statements attributed to Mr. Lesage were drawn from newspaper clippings. I hasten to indicate that what I have cited from the remarks of Mr. Lesage was taken from yesterday's press. Everything I cited appeared in quotation marks, and the words were attributed to the premier of Quebec.
(Translation):

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great respect and attention to the statement of the member for Megantic (Mr. Roberge) concerning an alleged difference between the statement made yesterday by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) and the answer which the premier of Quebec saw fit to give the press.
I am under the impression, Mr. Speaker, that the premier of Quebec somewhat misunderstood the statement made yesterday by the Minister of Finance concerning agreements between the federal and provincial governments on the matter of grants to universities. In my opinion, it has been clearly established in the house thanks to the action of the Conservative members from Quebec when Bill C-56 was under consideration last year that educational problems as well as the matter of grants to universities are an exclusive provincial prerogative.
The statement of the Minister of Finance yesterday did not go against the principle established last year, as a matter of fact the minister did not say that the government
Income Tax Act
was now prepared, before the agreements expire in 1962 to propose to the government of the province of Quebec another formula regarding university grants.
If we correctly understand the meaning of his words, we can see that the Minister of Finance clearly expressed in my opinion that the principle which has been recognized under Bill C-56, will be kept in force until 1962. So this arrangement in Bill C-56 shall remain in force for the province of Quebec until 1962, but the minister also indicated that should the province of Quebec be willing to discuss another form of arrangement after 1962, this government would be prepared to open discussions with the premier of Quebec.
I feel there has been a storm in a teapot over the statement made by the Minister of Finance, as well as the reply of the Quebec premier. An attempt has been made to muddle things up in order to gain political advantages.
I do not wish to express here the Quebec point of view, but I might say that, as long as the agreement under Bill No. C-56 is in existence, until 1962, we, on this side of the house, who represent the province of Quebec, will fight with the utmost energy to safeguard the principle that education should be the exclusive responsibility of the provinces, and that grants to universities be administered by the provinces, as provided under that arrangement.
And I am convinced that the Conservative party which achieved that compromise now helping Quebec universities, will manage, in the light of the discussions held, and whatever party may be in power in Quebec, to uphold that principle and recognize the claims of the province of Quebec.

Income Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I thank the house, Mr. Speaker. I simply wish to say something
by way of clarification of the matter raised by the hon. member for Megantic, which arises out of a statement I made in the debate in committee on July 10 and which has been commented upon by Premier Lesage of Quebec in a statement given to the press yesterday.
Mr. Speaker, it occurred in the discussion which you will find commencing at page 7813 of Hansard and principally at page 7817. It was concerning one clause of this bill, namely clause 19 relating to deduction from corporation tax in the case of corporate taxpayers in any province that is a prescribed province under the 1960 amendment. The position is this. I did not wish to give the committee the impression that I had discussed this particular bill with Premier Lesage. I did not wish to do that at all. What I indicated to the committee and sought to make very clear when the matter was raised a second time, as found at page 7817 of Hansard, was that the subject of the university grants and the special provision that had been introduced into the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act in 1960, in the case of any province which desired to become a prescribed province because its universities were not accepting these federal university grants, had not been introduced into the discussions at the conference; I refer to the dominion-provincial conference. My reference to my conversation with Premier Lesage, as I said in reply to a question by the hon. member for Laurier, was that this was a conversation that occurred outside the conference. I simply asked the premier whether he wished this subject to be introduced into the scope of the discussions in the conference. He indicated that it was not his wish. Clause 19 of the bill is consequential in nature simply by reason of the fact that the 1960 amendments to the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act which dealt with this subject were given only a two-year life. They conclude under the 1960 enactment with the conclusion of the

five-year period under the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act, namely March 31, 1962.
Before that date arrives there must of course be discussions in relation to how this problem is to be met in the future. That consideration was clearly in Premier Lesage's mind and it was clearly in my mind in what I said to the house on July 10. As found at page 7817 of Hansard, the first column, I stated as follows:
This matter as to what happens in regard to university grants will have to be a subject of further discussions between now and the end of this present fiscal year.
Again, as found at page 7818 of Hansard, at the top of the page, I stated:
I make it quite clear that we are not terminating anything. The hon. member-
That is the hon. member for Laurier.
-talks about our terminating something. We are not terminating anything. We take account of the fact that the legislation which was passed by parliament last year was given by parliament a two-year life. It will expire at the end of the present fiscal year. And all that we are doing here, pending the making of some new arrangement, is to make some provision for what happens at the expiry of that two-year term. It expires with the legislation that parliament enacted in 1960. I am not attempting for one minute, Mr. Chairman, to prejudge what may be done in relation to this problem as from April 1, 1962.
I make it quite clear, Mr. Speaker, that I think there is no occasion for misunderstanding on this matter. Certainly I did not wish, by anything I have said, to give rise to any misunderstanding in relation to either Premier Lesage's position or future discussions that may occur. This matter will certainly have to be discussed. At the present time the province of Quebec is a prescribed province under the 1960 legislation. Its federal corporate taxpayers received an additional 1 per cent abatement in 1960 and the province is continuing in the position, by its own decision, as a prescribed province also this year. Accordingly the federal corporate taxpayers in this province will receive the benefit of that additional 1 per cent abatement on corporation tax in 1961 as well.
As to what happens beginning with next year, that will have to be a matter for discussion. We shall be pleased, of course, to take this matter up with Premier Lesage and discuss it with him at any time that meets with his wish.

Mr. Speaker, the minister gave several citations from what he told us in the committee stage in the house, but he refrained from giving one which I now intend to put on the record. It is found at page 7813 of

Hansard, half way down, the first column, where the minister is reported to have stated as follows:
We were asked to leave out of this year's legislation, whether income tax legislation or federal-provincial fiscal legislation, any reference to the kind of arrangement that was made in 1960 and to provide for an alternative arrangement in respect of the university grants.

Premier Lesage.
My hon. friend from Megantic has read a statement by Mr. Lesage, who said he did not make that request. Those two statements are in direct contradiction of one another, and no discussion about what may happen in 1962 or any other aspect of the matter will alter that flat contradiction.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.
DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.
speechtext:
In speaking last evening to this resolution, Mr. Chairman, which deals with new tax sharing arrangements with the provinces, the minister had this to say, as found at page 7910 of Hansard:
It-
That is the new arrangement.
-has materially increased the return to the provinces from the existing tax sharing arrangements-
Then he also stated:
Although it has greatly improved the financial substance of the present arrangements, this government has recognized the weaknesses of the tax
Dominion-Provincial Relations
rental system which it inherited, both from the provincial and federal standpoint, and has become increasingly convinced of the need for a new approach which would give greater freedom and responsibility to the provincial governments, and which would be compatible with the constitution.
The minister then proceeded to show how greatly the provinces would benefit under these new arrangements. We do not propose to discuss the resolution at great length, Mr. Chairman. As I said last night, we will reserve our detailed consideration of this matter for the bill itself. However, if this new arrangement was so advantageous to the provinces as the minister indicates it was, it is very strange that the provinces, or at least most of them, should have been so ungrateful in their reception of it and so lacking in appreciation for this new deal. When these new arrangements were announced the premier of British Columbia expressed great disappointment that British Columbia would get no equalization grants, and he found other things to criticize in the arrangement. On February 27 the premier of Alberta told the Alberta legislature that the provinces of Canada were given "no option" at a federal-provincial fiscal conference in Ottawa on the Thursday and Friday before. He went on to say:
-the federal government left no door open for the provinces to choose between the new taxation program outlined them and the tax rental agreements presently in force.
Then he indicated his disappointment with these arrangements. That is two provinces. Then we come to Saskatchewan, where the provincial treasurer said on February 28 that the dominion-provincial tax sharing arrangements proposed by the federal government would not benefit Saskatchewan or its local governments. He then told the Saskatchewan legislature:
-the proposals would merely "freeze us to the level of payments we would have received under the present arrangements."
He went on to say this, according to the Canadian Press report:
Abandonment of the tax rental system means there can be no leadership expected from the federal government in preventing a return to the "tax jungle of the 1930's".
That is something I mentioned last night. Then Mr. Lloyd had this to say:
More important, it means the federal government will have lost the last vestige of control over the use of income taxation as a means for combating unemployment and stimulating economic growth.
So Saskatchewan was bitterly disappointed over these arrangements. Now we come to Manitoba, where the premier, according to a report in the Winnipeg Free Press, said this-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.
speechtext:
What date?

Dominion-Provincial Relations

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.
speechtext:
The date is April 8 and these words appear in an article by John Dafoe:
The new federal-provincial tax agreements which go into effect in 1962 won't likely produce any extra revenue for Manitoba until the 1964-65 fiscal year, Premier Duff Roblin told the legislature Friday.
The premier went on to say there were some good features in the agreement of which he approved. I do not wish to give a one-sided impression of his reaction. He also went on to say, and apparently this is the best Mr. Roblin could say:
"On the whole", Mr. Roblin said, "the new plan does Manitoba no harm at present and, in the latter years of the agreement it is likely to do some good through moderately increasing provincial revenues. It is, nevertheless, disappointing that the province is to receive no immediate increase in the new proposals as compared to the old agreements".
He also said this:
-"the lowering of the equalization level from the average of the top two provinces to the Canadian average would, by itself, seriously impair Manitoba's position".
Now we come to Ontario. As the richest province Ontario comes out of these arrangements better than any other province, but according to Premier Frost the arrangements fell-
-"far, far short" of the annual $150 million of additional revenue he had sought to negotiate in the two days of talks with Prime Minister Diefen-baker and Finance Minister Fleming.
Then he added:
"Additional taxes are our only possible alternative"-
We know what that meant; a sales tax. So the premier of the province that did the best out of these arrangements was singularly modest in his expressions of appreciation. So far as the premier of Quebec is concerned the Canadian Press story had this to say on February 24:
Premier Jean Lesage's first reaction to the news that his province would receive not a cent more from the arrangement was one of naked anger.
I think we can leave that reaction there. Then we get to the Atlantic provinces. Of course the reaction in three of the four Atlantic provinces was much more favourable. In New Brunswick the premier said the new taxation proposals "would do lasting harm" to his province. The premier of Nova Scotia -I wish to quote all the reactions, favourable and unfavourable-was more satisfied with the arrangements and expressed that satisfaction in measured terms. The premier of Prince Edward Island was satisfied. The premier of Newfoundland was pleased with the inclusion in the arrangement of the $8 million grant for five years in lieu of the constitutional grant flowing from act of union

under term 29. This is satisfactory, of course, as far as it goes, but it does not meet the point that this grant to Newfoundland was guaranteed by the act of union and should not depend on action by this parliament. However, there it is for five years, and I am sure the government and the people of Newfoundland will be very glad to receive it.
Mr. Chairman, this shows that in general the provincial reaction to the new tax sharing arrangements was not the kind one might have expected if in fact these proposals will do as much for the provinces as the minister indicated last night. To illustrate this the minister put some interesting tables on the record. As I said, we will in due course submit our own tables. There is one table to which I wish to refer particularly. That is table 3, which is headed:
Hypothetical illustration of provincial revenues for the year 1962-63 under new formula assuming-
This is the assumption that is made. I hope it is a more accurate assumption than others which have been made in this field by the minister:
-assuming rate of growth of 5 per cent per annum in tax yields and no change in the 1961-62 percentage distribution by provinces of tax yields or population.
I ask the minister now if he will also submit and put on the record a projection of this table for the four years after 1961-62. If these figures can be collected and made public for the one year, surely it is possible to do this for the subsequent four years of the agreement. We would certainly like to have that information, because without it the whole story is not told.
Our main quarrel with these new tax sharing arrangements and this new formula is the weakening of the principle and the application, of the principle of equalization. In this connection let me quote what the Prime Minister said on July 25, 1960 in words which surely constituted a formal pledge to the premiers of the provinces. The Prime Minister said this:
I want to make this abundantly clear on behalf of the dominion government that whatever the ultimate decision may be, the principle of equalization must be preserved.
No doubt the minister will tell us the principle is being preserved. But at that time the Prime Minister went on to explain what he meant by the principle and what he understood to be the application of the principle, which is even more important, when he defined equalization in these words:
-a payment by Canada to the provinces to bring the per capita return from the three taxes at standard rates up to the average per capita yield in the two provinces in which per capita yield is

highest. For provinces in which the tax potential is relatively low, this principle is most important.
By "principle" he meant bringing up the per capita yield in the other provinces to that of the two highest provinces, not the national average. This is a formal, specific, definite pledge and that pledge is abandoned for something else, Mr. Chairman, in these new arrangements.
This new formula has been put forward by the government in a form which I think could very easily deceive and which, indeed, has already deceived the layman, the nonexpert in this field. It appears to increase gradually the provincial share of personal income tax without, as the minister claimed last night, unduly weakening equalization. We claim that this impression is altogether unjustified. When we look at the new formula itself without the guarantees and the grants and the arrangements which were substantially attached to it, we find that only one province can benefit, and that is the richest province of all, and that all the other provinces will be worse off for the first few years during which the arrangements will apply, though that situation in some cases changes during the latter part of the agreement.
While the so-called new formula, then, would give $18 million more, I believe, to Ontario in the year 1962-63, all the other provinces would lose in that year as compared with the present arrangements in spite of the higher rates on personal income tax, through the lower equalization basis, because the basis of the two top provinces has been abandoned for the national average. Even though a new factor has been added, a new growth factor, nevertheless the receipts by the other provinces would be lower because of that fact.
Therefore what has been presented by the government as a new general formula is, at best, a formula which in the early stages would benefit the richest province only. Since the so-called general formula was clearly not applicable to all the other provinces, a lot of patchwork had to be done until we have these special arrangements, these special deals, if I may use that expression, designed to remove some of the original inequities.
There is a special grant, of course, to the Atlantic provinces. The existing grants are, I believe, increased by $10 million a year. But the Atlantic provinces will receive only $5it million more in 1962 and 1963 than they would receive if the present arrangements were continued, because of the application of the equalization formula. Of the additional $10 million which is provided, $4.5 million 90205-6-502
Dominion-Provincial Relations will be needed to fill the gap between the present arrangements and the new formula. It is only after four years that the Atlantic provinces will benefit fully from the additional $10 million, that is in 1965-66.
Then another arrangement is offered to Quebec, Manitoba and Saskatchewan, three provinces which will be below the national average for equalization purposes. That arrangement is a guarantee that during the next five years those provinces will not receive less than if the present arrangement had merely been extended. Under such a provision I admit that those three provinces will not be worse off. Quebec and Manitoba will begin to benefit slightly under the new formula in the last year of the new arrangements, that is in 1966-67. But Saskatchewan will never benefit during this period. These three provinces, therefore, will continue to live under the conditions of the existing arrangements during the next five years. For all practical purposes they will gain nothing; therefore their disappointment is easily understood.
Then, of course, a fourth arrangement is offered to Alberta and British Columbia, two provinces which would be above the national average. These two provinces do not receive less during the next five years than they got on the average during the last two years of the existing arrangement, that is in 1960-61 and 1961-62, as compared with the extension of the existing arrangements. However, as compared with an extension of the existing arrangements, Alberta will always be worse off under the new system. My calculation shows that Alberta will lose about $20 million in the next five years under the arrangement now contemplated. British Columbia will lose in the first two years and gain during the last three years. In the aggregate, if my calculations are correct, British Columbia will gain about $7 million during the next five years.
It is our contention that this new formula, these new tax sharing arrangements, weaken the principle of equilization; that they create rather than remove regional inequities as compared with the existing arrangements, and that these inequities will result from the lowering of the equilization base. Some of the provinces will be hurt. The per capita revenue in 1966-67, when the new system will yield its maximum benefits as compared to the present system, will be lower in Alberta, about the same in Quebec, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, and higher in the other provinces.
It must be observed also, and this is certainly important, that all the provinces in Canada under these arrangements will lose in relation to the richest province, the province of Ontario. Surely it is not a good thing for national unity, for one federal system and for national development to neglect to act

Dominion-Provincial Relations in a way which will bring the less rich provinces into alignment, as tar as that can be done by federal help, with the richer provinces.
These are the reasons why we disapprove of some of the aspects, and some of the important aspects, of this new program, and why we cannot go along with the minister in his extravagant praise of this new deal brought about after four years of conferences with the provinces; brought about, the hon. gentleman said last night, in a way which would cause great satisfaction in all the provinces which would benefit by it, but which seems to have been received in most of the provinces with disappointment and only in one or two with satisfaction.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.
speechtext:
It is the opinion of this group that this is by far the most important legislation which we have had before us since the house opened last November, because this has to do with the development or otherwise of the Canadian people as a nation.
As you know, Mr. Chairman, I represent a constituency in the province of British Columbia. I admit at once that I believe that in the long run, if we were to regain our original rights, or if our original right to levy our own levels of personal and corporation income tax were to be returned to us, British Columbia would be much better off than if the agreements were to be continued. However, I should like to think I was a Canadian before I was a British Columbian, and I believe most British Columbians would accept the responsibility of being Canadians ahead of any feeling they might have for their own welfare within the province.
We know that on a per capita basis we are one of the wealthiest and fastest growing provinces in Canada. We believe that the legislation forecast in this resolution is contrary to the intent of the fathers of confederation, who worked so hard and overcame so many difficulties to achieve the necessary teamwork and co-operation among the then existing colonies to lay the beginnings of one nation that was intended to extend from the Atlantic to the Pacific. We believe that in these proposals the government are not now supplying the leadership that is essential to the growth of Canadian nationhood. We believe they are supplying leadership in the wrong direction, and that this will hurt what we like to think is at least a developing nationhood.
We do not believe in centralization; we believe in the federal system of government. However, we now have responsibilities on all levels of government that were not even contemplated when Canada was first formed in 1867. I am sure if the fathers of confederation had been able to foresee the needs
of the Canadian people in 1961 they would have made many arrangements other than those that were arrived at. I am sure that were they here today they would not applaud the spirit that is behind the resolution now before us.
We do not want centralization. We need to continue, for very valid reasons, our federal concept of government. However, this ought not to prevent growing co-operation among all levels of government. This abrogation of the spirit of dominion-provincial tax sharing, this abrogation of the spirit of that legislation which we have had on our books now for so long, is not likely to lead to closer co-operation. It is more than likely to lead to greater divergencies, to greater discrepancy, to greater bitterness not only among various levels of government but also among various areas of Canada in their relationship one to another.
We realize that the path to harmony under our system of government is strewn with many obstacles indeed, that the difficulties are great; but we have confidence. We believe we have more confidence than the government of our day in the basic good intention and feeling of patriotism that exist in the hearts of all Canadian people from coast to coast. We feel that this legislation of desperation, as I would call it, is not crediting the Canadian people with the basic qualities that we believe they have. We contend that had there been a real will a way might have been found to resolve this problem in an altogether different manner from that that is now being proposed.
I know the minister is predicting all kinds of safeguards in the legislation to come before us so there shall be no undue hardship imposed on any of the provinces, but in essence what this government are proposing is that they are intending to desert a system whereby national agreement was reached and provinces were entitled to things as Canadians. That is to be replaced by what in effect is everybody for himself, and we shall in effect give hand-outs to our poorer relatives in other parts of Canada. I do not think the poorer provinces of Canada will take kindly to this new atmosphere that is to be created.
The people of Nova Scotia have rights as Canadians, and they do not want to feel that they are dependent upon the big-hearted Minister of Finance in Ottawa who may arbitrarily, in the years to come, have unto himself the right to determine the fate of the people of Nova Scotia, and be able to determine how much money we will be prepared to let the people of Nova Scotia have out of the national treasury.

We not only believe that this is a turning back of the clock with respect to the development of Canadian nationhood, but we also regret that this represents in essence a new low in our dealings with the provincial governments. We used to have the courtesy at least of sending them telegrams. The minister was severely criticized at the time he began to substitute the sending of telegrams to the heads of provincial governments for consultation. As the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate so rightly corrected me the other day, in effect in the atmosphere that now prevails the policy is "take it or else" and this has been made very plain. I was pleased to hear the leader of the official opposition say that at least the head of one government has complained that they have been left with no option, no open door. As I understand the language of no open door, this means that the federal government has decided in fact that there shall be no consultation any more to see whether agreements mutually satisfactory might not be arrived at. Now the provinces are told "take it or else".
In many respects it has to be "or else". If the provinces want to take advantage of federal collection machinery they will have to conform to very stringent and almost impossible conditions. I can tell the minister right now that if he insists on those conditions the province of British Columbia will have to collect its own income tax. It is absolutely unrealistic to expect a province that is as wealthy in natural resources, especially in the basic industries, to comply willingly with those terms. I am convinced that in its own interests the government of British Columbia will have to establish its own collection machinery. We in that part of Canada at least now know that we shall have a double system of income tax and in effect a return to the tax jungle of the hungry 1930's.
We believe the Minister of Finance of the province of Saskatchewan really hit at the essence of this policy when he said that the federal government is now proposing to abdicate its ability to combat recession and unemployment. What is going to happen? If the federal government decides that in order to stimulate the economy of our country a 5 per cent reduction in income tax is reasonable and desirable, the minister knows very well what the hard pressed provincial governments will immediately do. If the federal government for national purposes deems it advisable to reduce income tax levels by 5 per cent, each of the provincial governments will immediately absorb that 5 per cent and the intent of the federal government for national purposes will immediately have been vetoed. Vice versa, if 90205-6-5024
Dominion-Provincial Relations the federal government feels at some time that it needs to increase the levels of income tax there will be a great desire on the part of politicians on the provincial level to make good fellows of themselves, especially if they are politically opposed to the government at Ottawa. Their inclination will be to reduce the income tax by as much as the federal government raises it, so they will be able to go out on the hustings and say to the voters "Look what evil people the members of the federal government are; they have raised your income tax, but we good politicians, friends of the people, have lowered the income tax".
This will not lead to harmony. It will lead to disharmony. It will lead to one level of government being played off against another level of government. It will lead to the introduction of political aspects into this whole field, and the federal government will find that it has tied its hands with regard to its ability to accept responsibility for the national economic welfare.
The federal government will find that it has in effect deserted its responsibility with respect to the particular needs of hard hit regions of Canada. The federal government should realize that it is now proposing to desert the desire of all Canadians that there should be basic national minimum standards in the fields of health, education, welfare and highways, and that there should be teamwork in the matter of forest fires and so on.
I express the opinion that our nation is already far too deeply involved in the field of co-operation, in the field of the sharing of responsibilities between the two levels of government, for the federal government to attempt at this late date to turn back the tide. I should like to read one sentence from a book entitled "Law and Policy" by J. A. Corry, vice-principal of Queen's University and acting dean of the faculty of law. On page 62 he has this to say:
Federal spending now supports so much of the established political, social and economic structure that there is genuine reluctance to take steps that might wipe it out.
The book was published in 1959, and the passage I have read is taken from a lecture delivered by Professor Corry in 1957. I am sure that as recently as 1957 no leading thinker in our nation ever expected that the day would arrive when we would have in office a federal government that would attempt to push back the tide, that would attempt to turn back the clock; and I would say that the efforts of the government in this respect are going to fail because the Canadian people will not be prepared to accept this scheme.

Dominion-Provincial Relations
We have co-operation now between the federal government and the provinces in the field of combating forest fires, in the field of professional education, in the field of university education, in the field of highway construction, in the field of building forest access roads and roads to resources, and in the field of public welfare to ensure basic minimum standards for all Canadians. Every Canadian gets an old age pension of $55 a month no matter where he lives in Canada. Some Canadians receive more. They receive an additional payment from their local government, but every Canadian as a Canadian receives his $55 a month.
We have had for a long time the greatest of co-operation in the field of health and in our attempts to establish basic health services for all Canadians regardless of the province in which they live. The federal government is going to find it very difficult, if not completely impossible, to implement its apparent tendency to hand back to the provinces, as the government says, all the responsibilities and the revenues that constitutionally belong to the provinces. In the book "Law and Policy" some doubts are expressed as to the constitutionality of many of our existing activities where co-operation and the sharing of responsibilities with the provincial governments are involved. However, no leading Canadian has ever dared to test these things before the courts, and Mr. Corry comes to the conclusion that it is a good thing that the designation of particular responsibilities has been absorbed by the political field in Canada and that interpretations and rulings by the judiciary in this regard have been avoided. He feels that it is in the interests of a developing nation that this has occurred. He is rather pleased that political techniques have been employed to overcome at least a number of our major problems in this respect.
We cannot make uniform national progress in Canada if the intentions of the government are going to be pursued. We will find British Columbia becoming richer and Nova Scotia becoming poorer. This is inevitable. This measure will not supply employment to the unemployed miners of Cape Breton. It will not help northern New Brunswick to raise its living standards. It will make the people of Ontario wealthier than they are today, and possibly inadvertently and unintentionally it will result in the spread between the haves and the have-nots in Canada continuing to grow. We believe that the spread between the rich and the poor in the various regions of Canada in which they live should be narrowed. We understand that possibly not in our lifetime will all Canadians enjoy equal rights in all parts of Canada. However,


that certainly ought to be our objective; and the activities of this government in the matter of dominion-provincial tax sharing lead us in this group to believe that the government is leading us on to very dangerous paths indeed that will sow the seeds of disunity in Canada and will set Canadians against Canadians.
There is no appeal here to Canadians to come to the conference table and resolve their problems as Canadians. This is an appeal to Canadians to stay at home and ignore the welfare of other Canadians, who will have to make do; but in case they are in very dire need they will have the right to come to Ottawa and out of the goodness of our hearts we will then decide what kind of a hand-out we will give them to help them with their particular problems.
I cannot help but recall the underlying election appeal that our Prime Minister put forward so successfully in 1958. He really took hold of what he felt was a growing Canadianism, an awareness of Canadians as Canadians, and he capitalized on it very successfully on the hustings. I do not hold this against him. I suppose every politician likes to take the innermost feelings of the people and use them in order to commend his own election platform and program. I see nothing unworthy about that. However, I fail to understand how one great Canadian Conservative Prime Minister, Sir John A. Macdonald, could lead the first major move to weld the colonies into one Canada and another Conservative Prime Minister, who I am sure wants to be an equally great Canadian Prime Minister and who won election on the basic appeal to Canadianism, can now, instead of the co-operation we heard so much about, say to our provinces "Take it or leave it".
The government say, "We will give some guarantees to those of you who might otherwise have to suffer unduly, and if you run into serious difficulties we may, out of the kindness of our heart, decide to give you a hand-out." I am sure the founders of this nation meant that a Canadian would be a Canadian from the Atlantic to the Pacific. I deem it to be the responsibility of this gov-erment to ensure that a boy or a girl in Cape Breton will have the same educational and employment opportunities as a boy or girl in wealthy Ontario or wealthy British Columbia.
This government is steering this country in a direction that it was not intended it should go by those who founded our Canadian nation. If the Prime Minister warns of an election platform upon which he may be willing to appeal to the people, I can tell him that if he goes to the people now Mr. Coyne will have

been forgotten after the first week of the election campaign and this will be the big issue. I am sure we will win out on it.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I agree with what the hon. member for Bur-naby-Richmond has said, namely that this resolution takes us back to a period that could be characterized by saying that the taxing opportunities taken by the federal and provincial governments 20 years ago represented a period that was one of confusion and often of uncertainty. This resolution takes us back to the pre-Rowell-Sirois days before 1941. Anyone who is familiar with the history of federal-provincial fiscal relations will appreciate what that means. I also agree that this measure is calculated to bring about a lack of co-ordination in provisions for the standards of living of all Canadians. No matter what the minister may say to the contrary, it will mean that different provinces will have different means and methods of providing for the welfare of their people. There will be inequalities that will be encouraged as a result of the step that is taken in the government's policy embodied in this resolution and announced many months ago; it was announced last fall, to be precise.
However, one cannot fully appreciate the full implications of this resolution by merely examining its expressed provisions. In this resolution there is nothing to indicate the abandonment by the government of procedures that have been followed now since well after the beginning of the second world war. To understand exactly what the government has done one should go back to the assurances given to the Canadian people by the present Prime Minister when, in the opening campaign speech at Massey Hall on April 25, 1957, he said:
We intend to form a government to immediately convene a dominion-provincial conference to bring about a settlement of these problems, not in the spirit of arrogant domination as displayed by the present government, but in the spirit of unity and amity and with mutual tolerance and respect.
As was said by the hon. member who has just spoken, in this particular bill and all that it represents and all the procedures that were taken in connection with it from the time the government's present policy was announced there is nothing that suggests an

effort at unity or an effort at collaboration with the provinces. It is a "take it or leave it" position and is contrary to the spirit implied in the statement of the Prime Minister which I have quoted. In the same speech the Prime Minister said that he was pledged to work out new tax-sharing arrangements with the provinces which would strengthen Canada's federal system and give provinces and municipalities the funds to carry out their responsibilities.
It will be seen that this bill will not give the provinces the funds to carry out their responsibilities. It is therefore only right that at this late stage in our proceedings we should examine the implications of this resolution. As I said before the luncheon recess, when the bill comes before us there will be an opportunity to particularize our reactions to it. At this time, however, I wish to confine myself to one aspect of the consequence of this policy by giving special emphasis to its consequence in the province of Ontario.
It will be recalled that during the course of the present winter officials in the government of Ontario made it clear-and I may say this was early in February-that if they did not get the additional $100 million which Premier Frost said he must have from Ottawa, it would be necessary to impose a further form of taxation in the province of Ontario. As a matter of fact, I am wrong in using the figure of $100 million. While that figure represented the demand made a year and a half ago by Ontario, and also one made by the premier of Ontario in April of 1957, it had grown to not less than $118 million in the month of February of this year.
To understand the full implications of this resolution it should be recalled that in July, 1960 Premier Frost made additional demands on the federal government for a 50-50 share in federal income, corporation and succession duty taxes. At that time the proportion of sharing in these taxes by the provinces was on the basis of 13 per cent of income tax, 9 per cent of corporation tax and 50 per cent of succession duty taxes. Only because of the demands made on his government, Premier Frost pointed out, was it necessary for him to increase this amount. His enthusiasm in 1957 will be recalled, when he approved of this government and particularly of the present Prime Minister, giving every evidence that he fully expected to be able to obtain from the present federal government additional sums of money which he said had been denied his province by the previous administration.
While it is a fact that Premier Frost made his demand for an increase to 50-50 sharing in these three areas of taxation with the federal government, it is also a fact that this

demand was turned down by this government. It was turned down in a manner that 1 believe warranted the criticism Premier Frost and other members ol his government levelled against this administration for its failure to live up to the commitments made and the assurances given by the Prime Minister in his speech in Massey Hall in 1957.
When Premier Frost was faced with the rejection of his request for these additional sums of money, he then sought-it will be remembered-a constitutional amendment to give Ontario the right to levy an indirect retail sales tax. We do know that in October of 1961, the federal government, through the Prime Minister, said there would be no increase in the present sharing of tax revenues.

speechtext:
1 intended to say that in 1960 the Prime Minister announced there would be no increase in the sharing of revenues with the provinces beyond the formula of 13, 9 and 50 per cent. The Prime Minister then said that in view of the decision of this government not to increase grants as requested by practically all the provinces, the federal government proposed the abandonment of the existing tax rental arrangement with nine of the provinces.
The Minister of Finance has said that the proposal now before us was well received by the provinces. I think it is clear from what the Leader of the Opposition has pointed out that this is not the situation. The premier of Ontario had no hesitation in giving his reaction to this announcement of policy by the government. He said, "This is very far removed from Ontario's requirements. It falls far short". We do know that his dissatisfaction with this announcement of policy was widely shared all across Ontario. Perhaps a report in the Toronto Globe and Mail of March 6, 1961 reflects the reaction that exists throughout the province and which immediately followed the announcement by the Prime Minister. The Globe and Mail said on March 6, 1961:
What all of this shows to Ontario, and to the other provinces, is that leadership in fiscal matters cannot be left to Ottawa. Ottawa is not giving such leadership; will not give it for at least another five years, because the new tax sharing system which starts March 31, 1962 runs until March 31, 1967. By that time, the Ontario sales tax-like many another emergency measure-will be solidly entrenched.
The government of Ontario has announced that because of the failure of this government to live up to its commitments and its certain
Dominion-Provincial Relations failure to recognize the demands made by Ontario and other provinces, and because of the obligations imposed on the government of Ontario, it had to resort to an additional form of taxation to obtain the necessary revenues which it feels it is entitled to receive from Ottawa.
This is a far cry from the statement made by the Prime Minister in 1957 when he said, "We will make sure the provinces and the municipalities have sufficient money to do the job they are supposed to do". What the Prime Minister and what the government have in fact done is to say to Premier Frost and to the other provinces, "If you need more money, go out and get it yourselves". That is exactly what the province of Ontario has done.
I say that if the Ontario government has imposed a sales tax to be collected some time in the month of September, the main contributing factor in the decision of the Ontario government to provide for this additional form of taxation rests on the shoulders of this government because of the arrangement it is now proposing to the provinces.
I have before me the Ottawa Journal of February 23, 1961 and the headline is:
Sales tax threatened in Ontario.
The article goes on to say:
Such a tax, Ontario Premier Frost pointedly did not deny, could be the price of failure of the provincial and federal governments to reach an amicable new settlement of the 20 year old issue of tax sharing.
Let no one say that in suggesting the province of Ontario has been compelled to resort to this sales tax because of the failure of this government I am resorting to inaccuracy. This is based on an admission made by the premier of Ontario himself, as I have just indicated, in this story which appeared in the Ottawa Journal on February 23, 1961.
Mr. Chairman, we have also the budget of the provincial treasurer for the province of Ontario delivered by Mr. Allan on March 10, 1961 in which the provincial treasurer pointed out the need for additional revenue in Ontario. He pointed out the consequences of the failure of the federal government to recognize the claims made by Ontario and other provinces and then announced, of course, the decision of the government of Ontario to impose a sales tax.
It will be recalled that the provincial treasurer of Ontario had announced that his budget would be presented in the Ontario legislature some two weeks, I believe, or thereabouts, before the date when it was actually presented. It was postponed in the hope that as a result of the conference which was about to take place with the federal government there would be some announcement of policy by the federal government

Dominion-Provincial Relations which would enable the provincial treasurer to change his budgetary proposals. These changes were not forthcoming and in the budget of Mr. Allan of March 10, 1961 there was the announcement of this new policy and its consequences for the people of the province of Ontario.
I do not think I overstate the case when I say that throughout the province of Ontario there is great dissatisfaction over the introduction of this sales tax. I think when we are discussing this matter we should fix the blame where essentially it lies, as was stated by the provincial treasurer and by Premier Frost himself. The Ontario government said, "We need additional revenues. We cannot get sufficient moneys to take care of our obligations because of the failure of the federal government to give us the money to which we feel we are entitled. Consequently, as we have to build schools, as we have to build roads, as we have other obligations to meet, we have no other course but to impose this additional sales tax". I am not saying the Ontario government should not have found another way of providing for the revenues which it felt it required. I am saying that the evidence is clear; the Ontario government was driven into this position as a result of the position taken by the federal government and its intransigence with regard to its tax sharing policy with the provinces.
The consequence of this, in the province of Ontario, will, of course, be great. I mentioned the other day, and I repeat now, that the effects of the removal of the excise tax on automobiles at long last will be considerably mitigated in the province of Ontario, the largest market for Canadian purchases of automobiles, as a result of the sales tax to be imposed in Ontario collection of which will commence some time in September. The consequences will, of course, be even wider than this. They will be felt all over Ontario as this tax comes to be imposed on all kinds of goods, creating all kinds of new obligations for retailers and for consumers who, in their thousands, are beginning to protest the imposition of this tax. When we are discussing the policy of the federal government regarding this matter it is only proper that we should attribute to the federal government its share of responsibility for the course which has been taken in Ontario.
It is all very well for hon. gentlemen, when confronted with specific proposals, to examine them per se, to fail to relate them to the facts of history and to circumstances, particularly those which attended the announcement of policy by this government when it was asking the people of this country to give

it support in 1957 and 1958. We were told then that this government would embark on a policy which would resolve once and for all the fiscal differences which prevailed between the two senior levels of government. We were told there would be a dominion-provincial conference early in September. Those elections were held in the month of June. We know there was no conference held until the month of November, and then it was only because of prodding from this side of the house that a one day conference was held. We do know that following that conference instead of a policy being arrived at in collaboration with the provinces there was an announcement of the policy of the federal government, unilaterally, by way of a telegram which, we all remember, did not contain correctly the figures which had to do with further dispositions of money to be made to the provinces.
But let this be clear. We shall have an opportunity, when this bill comes before the house, of examining further aspects of this measure. The bill is not going to be dealt with until we return. We are now simply discussing the resolution. I feel, as a member from the province of Ontario, knowing the dissatisfaction which exists in Ontario over the sales tax, that it is only proper that we should attribute to this government the proper degree of responsibility for that fact. I do not say that this was the only way by which this additional money could be raised, but it is right to say that not only are individual citizens in the province of Ontario complaining, not only have members of opposition groups in Ontario complained about the sales tax, but organizations generally are complaining about the failure of this government to live up to its assurances in the matter of federal fiscal arrangements. When Ontario citizens come to pay this tax they will not only remember the Ontario government but they will remember the assurances given by the federal government -the assurances given by the federal Prime Minister in Massey Hall in the presence of Premier Frost in 1957. They will remember that Premier Frost indicated there was going to be some relief for Ontario as a result of a new fiscal deal.
Well, we have the results now, and there is no new deal for the province of Ontario. There is no new deal for the other provinces. What we have, once again, is a failure by this government to live up to the assurances which it gave not only to the people of Ontario but to the people of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this resolution is of extreme importance because it determines and establishes the axis around

which federal-provincial relations will revolve for a period of five years as of April 1, 1962, until March 31, 1967.
What are, briefly, the main points of this resolution?
An editorial published in La Presse of June 23, 1961, sums them up very well, I think, and I quote:
This week the Prime Minister communicated with the premiers of the provinces. He informed them that his government could grant them no more advantages than those offered in the taxation field during the last federal-provincial conference in February of this year.
In short, Mr. Diefenbaker had bad news for them.
The provinces in general and more particularly Quebec, were disappointed by the February conference on fiscal matters. After all, the provinces were still hoping that Ottawa would relent. Their hopes were now dealt a fatal blow.
As a matter of fact, Ottawa has regressed in the field of personal taxation. But it catches up in other ways, by amending the equalization formula. The new equalization formula submitted by Mr. Diefenbaker considers some new factors by which payments to Quebec will be, to all intents and purposes, frozen for the next five years, whereas, until now, they have been increasing rapidly from year to year.
The formula devised by Mr. St. Laurent was more generous, because it was based on the average return from the three normal taxes in the two wealthiest provinces, whereas the Diefenbaker formula is based on the average return of those same taxes in all provinces. Under Mr. St. Laurent, it was equalization from the top; with Mr. Diefenbaker, we have equalization from the bottom. From this point of view, the new proposal is not only less generous, but discriminatory.
Mr. Speaker, this resolution has been criticized for three fundamental reasons. First of all, the equalization principle is practically frozen, whereas it should necessarily remain adaptable and flexible. Second, the formula means equalization of provincial revenue from the middle instead of from the top, which led the Saskatchewan premier to say at the last federal-provincial conference that this was not equalization any more but "averaging". The premier of Quebec also had some concise but extremely revealing comments to make when he said that "the principle of equalization has been killed".
The third great weakness I see in this formula of the present government is that in practice, it means a greatly reduced income for the provinces recognized in the past as have-not provinces. Moreover, I feel quite sure that Mr. Duplessis would have been the first to reject such a formula outright. Why? Because at the last conference which he attended, he stated quite clearly that what
Dominion-Provincial Relations he wanted was cash; having little interest in the other formulas previously put forward, he would certainly not have liked this scheme which, in the case of the province of Quebec for instance, provides for reduced returns for the next five years, whereas under the old formula which was so bitterly attacked by our Conservative friends, the share of Quebec increased year by year.
In fact it will be recalled that for the first year Quebec drew an equalization payment of $36 million, and for the years 1960-61, it will draw approximately $72 million.
Referring to the table that was placed on the record yesterday by the Minister of Finance on page 7920 of Hansard, I find that it is a little over $71 million.
Mr. Chairman, it is well at this time, in order to understand the mechanics and the yield of both formulas-the old and the new-which are placed before us, to consider first the case of the province of Quebec as an example.
Under the old formula, it will be recalled that the yield of the three taxes, personal income tax, the corporation income tax and the succession duties, in the two most wealthy provinces, Ontario and British Columbia, was about $45 per capita. In Quebec, the per capita yield was $29, so that the province of Quebec was entitled to an equalization payment of $16, multiplied by its population figure. Now, the new formula that is placed before us takes into account the tax yield in the ten provinces, and that yield is about $34.50 per capita on a national basis, as against $29.50 in Quebec.
The province of Quebec is therefore falling short of the national average by approximately $5. Moreover, in this new formula, the government is introducing a new factor: the provincial natural resource revenue, more exactly 50 per cent of that special revenue. Now, the natural resource revenue per capita in the provinces comes to about $7.75, as against $3.25 for the province of Quebec.
Allow me to summarize the two situations. In the case of the three taxes, Quebec falls short of the national average by approximately $5, while in the case of the average for the natural resource revenue, Quebec falls short by approximately $4.50.
These two figures add up to a total of $9.50. And this $9.50, multiplied by the population figure of the province of Quebec, which is about 5,700,000, determines the equalization

Dominion-Provincial Relations payment to which we would be entitled, acording to the new formula proposed by Mr. Diefenbaker; it comes to some $47 million.
Therefore, that is much less attractive than the present formula which yielded approximately $72 million to the province of Quebec.
The Minister of Finance adds a guarantee that there will be no reduction in payments during the next five years. However, there is another guarantee, a guarantee we do not like, namely that during those five years those payments will not increase, as they would have if the old formula had been kept in force.
Mr. Chairman, in general the provinces have shown their disapproval, their great disappointment and their obvious dissatisfaction with that formula. That is why I feel the government is making a serious mistake in forcing the passage of this resolution, especially at this stage of the session. This matter is not urgent. The present agreements will expire only next spring and instead of arrogantly imposing its will to the provinces in a take it or leave it attitude, the government had ample time, to continue its negotiations with the provinces and to seek a new solution with them, in view of the importance of this matter for the unity and expansion of the Canadian federation.
I am not speaking here of expansion in the restrictive sense which the Minister of Finance gives to it, but in a broad sense which would allow the provision of essential services in all provinces so that there may be no underdeveloped sector and so that all Canadians may reasonably reach a comparable standard of living in all provinces.
The Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister have refused to budge an inch from the position they took at the last federal-provincial conference. Having expressed a refusal, they thought they could encourage the provinces by telling them: "Well, you can levy your own taxes if you are not satisfied", just as if that were a new right. In fact, certain provinces have already had to levy direct taxes as for instance, in Ontario where a 3 per cent sales tax will come into force next September.
If the government thinks it has given satisfaction to the provinces it is soon to suffer a rude awakening, after having promised so much to the provinces. It now introduces in resolution form legislation which is certainly nothing to boast about.
We of the official opposition have always attached a great deal of importance to the principle of equalization. But, for all practical


purposes, this measure is getting away from that principle. And the poorer provinces will be the most affected.
The Secretary of State, to comfort the province of Quebec, could tell her: You will get less under this formula, but you will gain in autonomy. He could also say: You will have a higher degree of autonomy than heretofore since you will be able to levy your own taxes should you need more money.
My concept of autonomy is quite different. It is a concept which reconciles constitutional rights and practical common sense. It is not by lowering equalization payments to the provinces in general and to Quebec in particular that we will be promoting their autonomy. A province can only exercise its autonomy to the fullest extent when it has all the required facilities to develop harmoniously. A municipality ceases to be autonomous when it can no longer face its obligations, and the same goes for the provinces, in similar circumstances.
Mr. Chairman, to put it briefly, I submit that this new formula is completely and directly contrary to the promises made to the provinces in 1957 and 1958. In addition to weakening the equalization principle, which has shown its value, this formula will leave the provinces in a state of discontent and frustration that will bring us much closer to fiscal disorder than to the agreement of 1867.

All these other stories that have been circulated as political propaganda by hon. gentlemen opposite show how little they have of a constructive character to say to the people of Canada.
What I am saying, sir, is that because of the attitude taken in 1956 at the time that the tax-sharing arrangements act was put on the statute books there was the greatest possible doubt in this country with respect to where the Conservative party stood so far as equalization was concerned. As the Minister of Finance has often told us, the opposition of that day, the Conservative party, voted against that bill. They talked against it and they voted against it and during all the period up to that time they said that they were in favour of a different system involving the allocation of tax fields. Mr. Drew was the leader of the party in the house at that time and he made many speeches on this subject. There was a legitimate fear in many quarters that if a Conservative government came into office in this country equalization would be done away with. The right hon. gentleman who is now Prime Minister will recall that in his speeches, and I think I have some extracts from them here which I do not wish to take up the time of the committee to quote-

The Prime Minister says they maintained the principle of equalization and they have maintained it precisely as it was expressed in Mr. Harris' bill in 1957. They maintained it right up until the month of October, 1960, I think it was. From November of 1957 when the first federal-provincial conference was held after the present government came into office until the conference held in July of 1960, the proceedings of which I have here in my hand, there was a good deal of speculation in the provinces and

Dominion-Provincial Relations elsewhere about what kind of proposals would be made to take the place of the existing Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act as amended and, to be completely fair about it as I wish to be, as improved by the present government. What was done in 1958 was an improvement and I have never pretended it was not at any time. I have once in a while ventured to express the view, and it is true, that it so happened that the only improvement that was made was made between the two elections. But that is true, of course, of everything else. There were quite a number of things done between the two elections but then the improvements stopped.
On July 25, 1960, a conference was held in the railway committee room in this building. It was opened by the Prime Minister and in the course of his remarks at that conference he made a statement which I should like to read into our record. I am going to read from page 10 and I do not feel I should do anything less than quote whole paragraphs although there are some portions of some of the paragraphs that really have nothing to do with the argument I am seeking to make. However, I wish to be completely accurate and completely adequate in what I say about what the right hon. gentleman said. He said:
Some provinces have indicated a desire to resume the collection of their own revenue from these tax fields.
I think it is in order to make the reference clear. That refers to the income tax, both personal and corporate, and the succession duty or estate tax.
This raises a question which will have to be considered in the course of this conference-
The question of some provinces wishing to resume the collection of these taxes themselves. The following are the words to which I wish to draw particular attention:
[DOT]-but I want to make this abundantly clear on behalf of the dominion government that whatever the ultimate decision may be the principle of equalization must be preserved.
