No, not at this moment- including the Leader of the Opposition, put on the statute books in 1956 when the Conservative party voted against it. This definition of equalization which the Prime Minister gave in very precise and very accurate language, was the principle of equalization about which he used these words:
I want to make this abundantly clear on behalf of the dominion government that whatever the ultimate decision may be the principle of equalization must be preserved.
Having said that, and so that there would be no doubt about it, the Prime Minister gave this definition of equalization which I have just read. Then, having said that, he also said this:
The government believes that the principle of fiscal aid and equalization to assist the less wealthy provinces stands on its own feet and is accepted on that basis, and is quite separate from the question of tax rental or tax sharing.
I think that is a principle with which no one would have any quarrel. I do not know that they need necessarily be separated in the statutes. In fact, they never have been and are not going to be now under the proposals before us. The fact is that they are two different elements of the matter and the Prime Minister rightly pointed that out. I have no quarrel with the statement made by the Prime Minister. In fact, the contrary is true. I went to that conference and I listened to that speech because I have always been greatly interested in this subject. I recall that day saying to a friend of mine who was with me, now at last one thing is quite clear and that is that the present government has accepted, in unqualified language,

Dominion-Provincial Relations
the principle of equalization as it is understood and as it is clearly defined. This is something on which the provinces can really rely. Well, the provinces relied upon it for how long? I believe it was from July until October.
Then, in October 1960, the Prime Minister came along at the next stage of the conference with what he was pleased to call a suggestion. This suggestion repudiated this definition of equalization that the Prime Minister had solemnly affirmed in July. If I may use his own words, he said:
I want to make this abundantly clear on behalf of the dominion government that whatever the ultimate decision may be the principle of equalization must be preserved.
This was not some vague principle, but was equalization as specifically and carefully defined by the Prime Minister in that paragraph to which I referred.
Then, in the month of October the Prime Minister came along with this suggestion, this new mix, which imported into the principle of equalization the notion of revenues from natural resources and the national average instead of the average of the two highest provinces, which was the principle of equalization the Prime Minister had undertaken to preserve. I say that if anybody understands the word "repudiation" in its ordinary meaning, this was a very clear repudiation in October. We described it as such from this side of the house and we have consistently so described it ever since. It was a repudiation of a solemn undertaking given to the premiers of the provinces at that time. This is a repudiation of a principle that was evolved and, as I said the other day when speaking on the income tax bill even Mr. Duplessis, with all his intransigence admitted, after the conference of 1955-56, that the principle of equalization was a great improvement on what had previously existed. This principle had been patiently evolved over the years, and now it has been repudiated.
We had, first of all, what was delicately called a suggestion in October, what became a proposal in February and what is now a "take it or else" attitude as indicated by this resolution. Without going into any of the details, sir, that is the record of this government so far as equalization is concerned.

I say, sir, that this is a sad and sorry way to deal with a problem that was nearer solution in 1956 than it had ever been. The house resumed from Friday July 7, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-71, respecting the civil service of Canada-Mr. Fleming (Eglinton)-Mr. McCIeave in the chair.
On clause 1-Short title.

Mr. Chairman, when I was speaking on this bill on the last day when it was before this committee, I had listed some of the advantages that will be made available by the bill if passed by the house to the civil service and to the civil service administration of the country generally. I had mentioned that under Bill No. C-71, the right to pay of employees of the government is recognized for the first time and that a wide system of appeal is now available to civil servants from administrative decisions within the departments in which they work. I had mentioned that the distinction between temporary employees and permanent employees has been removed and that now there can be a transfer from the public service to the civil service in appropriate cases. I had also mentioned that a very real preference will be set forth under the bill for bilingual people and that the bill provided for the admission of new Canadians to the civil service who under the old act were prohibited from giving service to the country in this way. I had come to the point where I was talking about the very major gain in the new relations between the civil service and the government in the provision of a consultation method and procedure and also the discussion in the committee as regards the setting up of arbitration facilities where disputes might arise.
In that connection may I say this. When the hon. member for Hull was speaking on Thursday, July 6, he said as follows:
The minister has referred to arbitration. He referred to it as something highly dangerous. He said he opposed it because he wanted to protect the rights of parliament.
This appears at page 5 of the translation of the debates of July 6. The hon. member was referring to the Minister of Finance at that time. I bring this to the attention of the committee because it is so palpably wrong and unfair, that it should not be allowed to go unchallenged. Actually when

the minister was before the committee he stated as follows, and I am referring now to the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the special committee on the Civil Service Act at page 537:
We do not wish to embark on any radical or untried form of legislative action, but we-I speak for my colleagues and myself-are willing to explore the possibility of developing in Canada procedures based upon precedent and fortified by good faith. I think it is recognized by all, Mr. Chairman, that any system of negotiation which might be considered will require considerable time, and no doubt patience, to develop along these lines. I am led to believe that the views of the staff associations themselves on matters of representation fall somewhat short of unanimity. I would respectfully suggest, therefore, that this whole question be carefully explored so that the rights of parliament will not be unduly abridged, and that all of us on our part and in our turn will be able to develop an approach to the question of consultation on matters of pay and conditions of employment which, being based upon precedent and experience, will stand the test of time.
That is certainly the opposite of the impression that was left with the committee by the hon. member for Hull.
Further, I find a completely different interpretation from that put upon the minister's words by the hon. member for Hull in a column written by Mr. John Stockdale of the Ottawa Journal, in the issue of that paper of Saturday, June 24. Mr. Stockdale followed the meetings of the special committee very closely and he as much as anyone is familiar with the bill and what it intends to achieve. What Mr. Stockdale wrote is as follows:
It may not all be spelled out in the new Civil Service Act, but the writing which will concede powers of negotiation and arbitration within the Canadian civil service is on the wall-if not in the bag.
The prophets who put it there are no less than finance minister Fleming and parliamentary secretary Dick Bell.
Reactions from staff organizations today are generally favourable, even if there are reservations related to the circumstance that techniques of discussion and negotiation remain loosely defined.
Mr. Fleming made it clear consultation with staff associations on pay and conditions was to be at all appropriate times. Mr. Bell was emphatic that, in a relatively short time, it was intended to achieve a Canadian version of Britain's Whitley procedure -and the cornerstones of the Whitley system are negotiation and arbitration.
The need to avoid legislative rigidity was stressed. If the elastic seams now incorporated within the bill are stretched sufficiently, most of the objectives of the major staff associations can be attained.
An established means of working together in harmony, understanding, mutual confidence, good faith. That was what Mr. Fleming regarded as the shape of things to come.
Neither the inquiring Liberals on the committee nor the staff associations could-if principle works out in practice-want more.
On June 28, after the committee had concluded its sittings on the bill and after the statement of the Minister of Finance had been
Civil Service Act
placed on the record, a press release was issued by Mr. Fred Whitehouse, president of the civil service federation of Canada. As all hon. members know, the civil service federation of Canada is by far the largest of the civil service staff associations and embraces some 80,000 civil servants. I quote from the press release of Mr. Whitehouse:
-it is apparent that the government in providing for compulsory consultation has moved a long way towards giving public servants a voice in determining their rates of pay and conditions of employment. This is especially true in view of the statements made by the Minister of Finance in committee that it was expected that the provisions for consultation would evolve into a system modified to meet the needs of the Canadian civil service, similar to the Whitley councils of Great Britain. Mr. Fleming felt this could be done without the restriction of legislation.
The minister went on to say that an important element in negotiation and consultation on these matters is to meet in a spirit of good faith and co-operation on the part of both sides. The civil service federation of Canada agrees with this statement and is prepared to meet with the civil service commission and officials of the government in a spirit of co-operation and good faith, always bearing in mind that co-operation is a twoway street and good faith on both sides must be the vehicle employed to reach our mutual destination.
The civil service federation of Canada agrees to the foregoing with a view that experience will lead both sides to the evolution of a system of negotiation and arbitration in the shortest possible period of time.
I also had a letter from Miss Frances E. Goodspeed, president of the professional institute of the public service of Canada. This is another of the large civil service staff associations, embracing I believe some 5,000 civil servants. This letter, dated June 27, 1961 reads as follows:
Dear Mr. MacLellan,
On behalf of my colleagues in the professional institute and myself may I express our appreciation of the opportunity which was afforded us to appear before your parliamentary committee on Bill C-71 and the careful consideration of our views on the subject matter of this bill by the committee.
Members of the professional institute who attended the sessions of your committee were greatly impressed with the very thorough and searching review which was given every section of the bill. We are confident that your efforts will result in a new Civil Service Act which will afford an opportunity to continue in the future the development in Canada of a public service which will give the utmost satisfaction to the public in the discharge of its duties, personal satisfaction to those who seek therein a challenging and useful career, and which will gain even greater regard abroad than it currently enjoys.
I believe that in yesterday's press there appeared an account of an interview with Miss Goodspeed wherein she stated that she was very satisfied with the progress that had been made toward the beginning of a system of arbitration for the civil service. I would

Civil Service Act
point out that in the meetings of the special committee there was at no time any suggestion that arbitration should not be something which we could look forward to in the future. There was a difference of opinion as to method. There were some who thought that by legislation we could accomplish arbitration more quickly, but the majority of the committee was of the opinion and agreed with the Minister of Finance that arbitration could better be gained by evolution, as was done ..in the United Kingdom, without direct legislation. I believe the passages I have quoted indicate that the majority of civil servants take the same stand.
In addition to the matters which I have mentioned, an eighth advantage to the civil service provided by the bill is in the establishment of a grievance procedure. This is another measure which the civil service has been requesting for many years. We were very pleased in the committee to amend this bill to provide for the establishment of a grievance procedure. This is something which I believe will also assist in the development of better relationships between the government and the civil service.
All in all, Mr. Chairman, I feel this new bill which is before the committee should be passed as soon as possible, as was requested by Miss Goodspeed in her statement of yesterday. By virtue of the bill a new, golden age will be ushered in as regards the relationships between the people of Canada and their civil service. Most of the problems have been removed and I am sure that the days ahead will illustrate the value of this bill to the civil service and the work they do for our country.
In closing, Mr. Chairman, I should like for a moment to pay tribute to the hon. member of the special committee who attended every meeting; who more than any other member of the committee carried the responsibility and the burdens of this bill; who more than anyone else understands the problems of the civil service and, I believe, who more than anyone else can be called the champion of the civil service in Canada. I refer to the distinguished hon. member for Carleton, the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance, with whom it was my pleasure to work very closely during the months we were considering this bill.
I am sure hon. members on all sides of the house will endorse what I say, that the hon. member for Carleton is one of the finest lawyers and parliamentarians we have in the house and certainly is the best friend in court that the civil service has ever had. If I may say one thing to the civil service of Canada, and in particular to the civil servants who

live here in the Ottawa valley, it is that the best way to strengthen their own causes is to strengthen the hand of the hon. member for Carleton.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Chairman, I am not going to try to compete with hon. members who have preceded me in congratulating the members of the committee and the chairman, except that I must say all congratulations offered to the chairman were well deserved. The committee proceedings were conducted fairly and well. I must also say that all members of the committee, and not only the hon. member for Carleton, were great friends of the civil service and were trying to do their best to ensure that the civil service of Canada would have a good deal.
I should also add that those who appeared before us were most helpful. I refer to the members of the civil service commission, the representative of treasury board, the members of the staff associations and those who sent in letters on certain problems for our perusal, including the question of bilingualism. These representations were very helpful. The meetings were conducted in a spirit of fairness and I think this is one committee which could serve as an example to some others which have sat during this and other sessions of parliament.
However I do not altogether give the credit for this to those of us who sat on the committee. It so happens that we were a group of dedicated people who were considering a very delicate cause. This legislation which is designed to improve the civil service is most important because in our time more than ever before a good civil service is absolutely essential to good government. The need for a growing and better qualified civil service can be attributed primarily to the increased role of government. As a result we have to rely more and more on an increasing number of experts and highly qualified administrators. The civil service in Canada is composed at all levels of men and women who are well qualified to perform their important functions and who are devoted to the service of their country, people who are entirely loyal to the government of the day. Those who give loyalty and service have a right to expect confidence, support and encouragement, in addition to conditions which will make them more effective in their work.
This bill is the result in part of investigations which began in 1957 with the then chairman of the civil service commission, Mr. Heeney, and his associates who were asked to make a report on the Civil Service Act.

That report was very full and it was discussed in committee last year. In part this present bill implements some of the recommendations of the Heeney report. However,
I do not want anyone to think that this bill implements the whole of that report. I should just like to put on record the case for a new concept in law which the chairman put in his report in 1958. He said:
The legal framework within which a public service functions is of importance because of its direct bearing upon quality and administrative efficiency. Law alone cannot guarantee good administration but it can and does have a real effect on the quality of the personnel who are recruited and it can provide incentives to good performance. As conditions change, there develops from time to time a need to re-examine legislative arrangements so as to determine whether the law is well suited to current needs. Forty years ago, the need was for a civil service free from what Sir Robert Borden called "the malign influence of patronage". Forty years ago, and this is all too frequently forgotten, the need was also for a public service free from nepotism, the coddling of incompetent favourites, the granting of promotions for consideration and similar internal abuses. Not much is gained if the "malign influence" of political patronage is replaced by bureaucratic patronage, which may be less apparent but which can be no less insidious and demoralizing. If both are to be kept in check, there is need for independent authority and control such as the commission was designed to provide. The effectiveness of the present act in protecting the national service from these traditional abuses is a convincing argument for the preservation of the essential legal safeguards of the merit principle. At the same time, in the vastly different social and economic conditions within which public administration must be conducted today, it has become evident that a monolithic merit system is not in itself enough.
Those were the broad principles of the Heeney report. As I said before, the Heeney report is adopted in part in this bill, but only in part, as we shall have the opportunity to see when we examine the clauses one by one. In case hon. members may be under a misapprehension let me say that this bill is not what could be called a bold, new approach embodying new principles. In many ways the bill is a 1961 version of the 1918 act in the light of practices which have developed over the years. It does not attempt, for example, to provide new and broad principles governing personnel administration and employer-employee relations which the service needs and which the service requests. This is probably one of the points of real importance which came up for discussion in the committee when it dealt with staff association representations. While clause 7, which embodies the principle enunciated by the government in this regard is a great advance, we must express our stand at this time and say that the principle involved in this bill in this regard is not satisfactory to the opposition. The time has come to face
Civil Service Act
the issue of bargaining between the government and its employees squarely and frankly. As I said on March 7, in our country all municipal employees, including policemen and firemen have obtained the right to collective bargaining. In the federal field the majority of the employees of crown companies already enjoy such a right. But ordinary civil servants have no right whatsoever in this respect. This has become a serious anomaly and an unfair discrimination. In Great Britain, Australia and New Zealand the right to collective bargaining has been granted in one form or another to civil servants. In the United Kingdom, the national Whitley council agreement on arbitration for the non-industrial civil servant has now been in force for more than 30 years.
Our stand on this principle is still the one that I expressed some months ago. We believe that the present Canadian system which provides only for consultations-and that, after all, is all that is included in the present bill-[DOT] is completely inadequate to protect the fundamental right of the civil service to participation in collective negotiations. At the same time, our view is that the right to strike should not be granted to the civil service and that a strike should not be tolerated in the government service. We believe that civil servants should be granted the right to joint negotiations and arbitration provided the supremacy of parliament is safeguarded.
We do not intend at this stage to put forward a concrete and detailed proposal which would embody these rights, but I suggest- and this is in accord with proposals I made in the committee-that consideration of the question should be given in the present bill and that details should be worked out by negotiation and by arrangement between the staff associations and representatives of the government. Surely, if it has been possible to do so in other countries, and in one province within Canada, it is possible to do tbe same in the federal field. The act presently in force goes back to 1918, which is some 40 years ago. Surely, we shall not have to wait 40 years before our ideas become a little bit modern-we shall not have to wait that length of time to see whether the procedure enunciated in clause 7 of the present bill is satisfactory.
There are a few other points which come to notice, but I do not intend to deal with them at the present time. One is the increased power given to deputy heads of the departments under this bill. In this connection I should like to refer to the submission by the professional institute of the public service of Canada. In the last paragraph on page 1 it is stated that the point of

Civil Service Act
concern is the trend toward delegation or transfer of authority from the civil service commission to deputy heads in matters concerning personnel selection, establishment, etc. The professional institute believes that certain rearrangements along the lines indicated will result in increased efficiency and therefore welcomes the proposal from this viewpoint. It has, however, become increasingly apparent to the institute over recent years that even the existing degree of local autonomy within and between departments has markedly affected conditions of employment. It is felt that any further decentralization of authority in the field of personnel management has to be accompanied by a system of monitoring and control much more effective than presently exists. Lacking such a system, the advantages of increased departmental initiative would be negated by damage to morale and even to the merit system itself.
Another aspect of this bill is the power which remains to dismiss any employee without cause. Of course, there may be some good reason for this revision but we were not told in the committee why such a power should remain in the bill. Of course, I shall have an opportunity to say something about that when we reach the relevant clause.
Another factor is that prevailing rate employees should somehow not be considered in this legislation. A way should have been found to treat them as other civil servants have been treated and bring them within the Civil Service Act. They should be given all the privileges enjoyed by other civil servants. This is an anomaly and a difficulty which we might as well face now.
There is another difficult problem which will arise during the discussion of the bill, namely the right of appeal. All of these things, Mr. Chairman, depend to a great extent on the regulations which will be made under the legislation. It is very difficult to discuss the effect of many clauses of this bill without knowing what the regulations are to be. When we were in committee I did raise the point that the regulations should have been brought before us for consideration. I was told that they had been drafted but the committee did not see them. Therefore, we cannot take any responsibility for any of the regulations which have been drafted already and which may form part of the legislation after it is passed.
I raise these few points at this time, Mr. Chairman, because we shall have ample opportunity to raise other matters of importance when we discuss the clauses. However, I welcome the improvements which have been made in the present act.

I have only this to say. Once again I repeat, the staff associations deserve our thanks for the manner in which they effectively presented their case. I must say that it would be much better if they united some day. If they could have one broad association representing all civil servants perhaps they could make their case much more effective.

Mr. Chairman, since this bill was introduced we have had many individuals posing as the special friends of the civil servant. I know there are many members in this house who have had special duties in connection with these problems and who have a great many civil servants within their riding. However, I do think it is time to put in a word of caution on behalf of the long suffering taxpayers in this country. It seems to me that when the change in government took place in 1957 one of the complaints of the people was not just that the cabinet had become too hard to get along with or that the Liberals had got too arrogant. The whole service had got a little too stuck in that way of doing business. In some respects it had taken on some of the characteristics of its bosses, and. a complete change was needed. If I may say so, what has been said to me most often since I became a member of parliament is this. Those who have spoken to me have said that they did not see that change in attitude that they had hoped to see when we took over, or at least they did not see it change as much as they had hoped. I am speaking now just of people completely outside the civil service who have talked to me. The main complaints I have had about the failure to make a sweeping change in the civil service came to me from people within the civil service. There are in that organization, as there are in other organizations, the extremely intelligent, the extremely hard working and the ordinary. There are the loafers, as there are in other jobs.
The main source of their complaint seems to be that the method of doing business had become so stereotyped that the rule book and the way of doing things had become predominant. The attitude of "this is the way we do it; this is the way we have been doing it for years," had become so important that the ambitious, hard working civil servant found entirely too many stumbling blocks in his road to do the job as efficiently as he would wish. I repeat, Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention here today to complain about the civil service. I merely think it is necessary to point out that there is such a thing as giving the civil service too much protection from public opinion, by laying down the rules too hard and fast so that they become all-important, so that their main

function seems to be how to preserve, protect and extend their method of doing things as they have done them over the years rather than concentrating on the fact that they are there for the service of the public, and giving them more leeway to find more ways, and more efficient ways to be of benefit to the public.
For instance, I noticed that with respect to a change in position the legislation reads, "The deputy head recommends to the commission". I am very much afraid that this sort of provision is going to perhaps aggravate the sort of trouble about which the conscientious civil servant has complained to me.
After a good many years in the service there is bound to be the feeling "We have done this for years and we have done it this way", and even to the most honest and conscientious department head the suggestion by some of his staff, new staff particularly, that a new and more efficient method of doing things can be found is likely to be met with a good deal of resentment. If the department head happens to be a very intelligent man and a big man he is going to take it in stride; he is going to look at the suggestion very carefully, give the man credit and make sure that even a refusal of the suggestion is not going to discourage that employee from looking for improved ways of achieving more efficiency. If, however, the department head concerned happens to be an individual who has moved up despite his lack of ability over a great many years and who has become more and more set in his ways, the mere possibility of making a suggestion of changing the old method is going to leave that employee in a very awkward position in the department for a long time.
I am suggesting that it is not enough that the job be done in a certain way. It may very well be that the old method of doing things is very efficient; it might even be the most efficient way; nevertheless, the business of government is not run just like an adding machine. The government is always dealing with the citizens of this country and their feelings must be respected. I venture to suggest that it is not the business of this or any other government, or of the civil service, to continue to try to ram down the throats of the ordinary citizens those procedures that the ordinary man in the street finds annoying day after day, even if those procedures may be most efficient. I suggest that we have had too many barriers between the civil servant and the person he is serving, namely the ordinary taxpayer of this country. It has been most unfortunate in many respects; it has hindered the work of the civil service to this extent, that the taxpayer has failed to
Civil Service Act
understand the civil servants and the civil servants have failed to understand the taxpayer. This lack of understanding has often resulted in a lack of co-operation, which hinders efficiency and which leads to bad feelings all around.
I am suggesting, Mr. Chairman, that if we insulate the civil servant too much from the minister who is after all responsible for having his finger on the pulse of the people, we are making it more difficult for the civil servants to perform their duties in a way which will please the public. It is more difficult for them to realize when the public are pleased and when they are not. I suggest, therefore, that the theory of protection of the civil servant from the politician has gone a little too far. We have, I suppose, to protect the civil servant from some politicians under some circumstances but I am suggesting to the committee that the putting up of more barriers is adding to the concept of the civil servant as something distinct and separate from the people. It has made his job more awkward and those who have talked to me have not liked the idea that they have been criticized by so many people over the years when they have been trying so hard to do their jobs. There is, I suggest, a lack of understanding, and I wish that we would allow just a little political influence to enter the picture so that civil servants can get closer to the people in understanding.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I want to say a few words on this measure because I have noticed that bilingualism gets a better deal under this bill. Here is what I see in clause 47 of the bill:
The number of employees appointed to serve in any department or in any local office of a department who are qualified in the knowledge and use of the English or French language or both shall, in the opinion of the commission, be sufficient to enable the department or local office to perform its functions adequately and to give effective service.
This clause represents a big improvement over the former act as far as bilingualism is concerned. I do want to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) for it.
We are all aware of a brief submitted by the conseil de la vie frangaise, which dealt with the situation of French speaking Canadians in the federal civil service. Here, from 1950 to 1958, the departments where the proportion of French speaking Canadians has increased are the following:
Veterans affairs, 3.2 per cent; agriculture, 1.1 per cent, but with substantial decreases in some services. In the auditor general's office,

Civil Service Act
the increase has been of 10 per cent, but the staff there is very limited, so that the increase is slight there also; R.C.M.P., 1.1 per cent; fisheries, 1.3 per cent; national revenue, 1.6 per cent; secretary of state, 9.3 per cent; labour department, 1 per cent; national film board, 9.1 per cent.
On the other hand, there has been a decrease in the proportion of French-speaking Canadians, in the same period from 1950 to 1958: external affairs, 0.4 per cent; citizenship and immigration, 2.5 per cent; trade and commerce, 2.6 per cent; civil service commission, 2.6 per cent; national research council, 0.9 per cent; national defence, 1.2 per cent; finance, 0.6 per cent; printing bureau, 20.3 per cent; justice, 5.8 per cent; mines and technical surveys, 0.7 per cent; Post Office Department, 11.8 per cent; resources and development, 2.6 per cent; health and welfare, 6 per cent; transport, 2.1 per cent; public works, 16.8 per cent.
Mr. Chairman, I have taken those figures from the brief submitted by the conseil de la vie frangaise in which we find statistics for the period going from 1950 to 1958.
As I said a while ago, this bill is an improvement on the present act. It will encourage my people, the French Canadians, to apply for positions with the civil service in Ottawa. In my opinion, it is essential, in the interest of national unity, that nearly one third of the positions in the civil service-not only secondary positions, but key positions- be held by French-speaking or bilingual Canadians.
In a few years we will celebrate the centenary of confederation. It would most certainly be appropriate, in the interest of national unity, first that a greater number of my people apply for positions in the civil service-that is most important-and second, that a greater number of French Canadians be appointed to key positions in the federal service. It would certainly be possible to improve the situation so as to attract both English speaking and French speaking Canadians to the civil service and to make them better qualified to work for the Canadian government.
I wonder whether it would not be appropriate to consider the possibility of establishing a civil service school to train both French speaking and English speaking Canadians to work for the government. Such a school could be established by the civil service commission or by the Secretary of State department.

Moreover, although education comes under provincial jurisdiction, it would be a good thing if Canadian universities, and especially those from the province of Quebec, had a department where French-speaking candidates would be trained for positions with the civil service in Ottawa. In fact, if Canadian universities had such a department, we would have better trained civil servants.
We would then have better qualified people, something which, apart from being in the interest of national unity-it is always desirable to have a logical proportion of Frenchspeaking and English-speaking Canadians- would enable the country to have more qualified men to serve the Canadian people.
Mr. Chairman, those are the few remarks I wanted to make.

As a member of the special committee whose task it was to study the Civil Service Act, I think it is my duty to point out that the bill we have before us constitutes an improvement over the present Civil Service Act which, as everyone knows and as several members have said previously, had not been revised since 1918.
Mr. Chairman, I heard a moment ago some members of the opposition make statements on the civil service and on the fact that the bilingual civil servants are less numerous now than before. These members seem to forget that during the 22 years they were in power they did not improve that situation, far from it, as I will show in a few moments. On the other hand, the bill before us is calculated to correct this anomaly, thanks to a quite special clause which my colleague the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Mont-calm (Mr. Pigeon) has quoted and which I will discuss briefly in a few moments.
Mr. Chairman, we all agree that the part civil servants play in the administration of this country is becoming increasingly important, and that they are the ones who, in any well organized government, are responsible for research and study on which is based the government's policy and its preparation at the first stage, as well as the administration of the legislation passed by parliament. In fact, it is on them that we rely for these collective services which are, so to speak, the reason for the existence of the state.
They are also charged with the administration of controls, the collection of taxes, the spending of public funds; in short, they have an executive role given to them by the government in power.
[Mr. Hicard.l
The civil servants have always played a most important part not only in the administration of the country but also in the administration of each province and municipality.
As, nowadays, the responsibilities of the government are continuously increasing in the economical and social life of a country, and becoming more and more complex, the responsibilities of the civil servants are bound to take an increasing importance, and more and more civil servants are required all the time.
I do not have before me the last statistics concerning the total number of civil servants but, if my memory serves me right, I believe that there are more than 200,000 federal civil servants, irrespective of the staff of the crown corporations or of other departmental agencies which employ nearly 150,000 people.
It goes without saying that I am not including the members of the armed forces in these statistics.
On the other hand, Mr. Chairman, the citizens, and especially businessmen and professionals, must constantly keep in touch with the government administration.
Therefore, they take an immediate interest in the competence, efficiency, sympathy and understanding of civil servants. That is to say that the efficiency of the country's administration and the good relations between citizens and the government are at stake. This principle of efficiency in administrative services is based on the relations between the state and its servants.
In the course of its various meetings, the committee received many representations from different staff organizations. Their representatives had the opportunity of expressing their views and they were questioned by members of that committee.
I too should like to offer congratulations to the committee chairman who so ably conducted the proceedings and join with previous speakers who mentioned the matter.
I do not intend to point out all the evidence submitted before that committee, because hon. members will be able to read the various reports that have been published, but I should like to stress a few points and especially the one which was raised a while ago by the hon. member for Edmonton-Strath-cona (Mr. Nugent) and which deals particularly with the power given to deputy ministers under the present bill. I share his opinion. Indeed, I think the various organizations have made recommendations along those lines, namely that the bill grants exceptional powers to the deputy ministers. I am not saying

that the latter will abuse those powers or that some deputy ministers have done so in the past; I have not been in the house long enough to make such a statement. However, it could give rise to certain difficulties between civil servants, that is between higher officials and their subordinates.
1 wish to refer to a recommendation which was made by the conseil de la vie frangaise d'Amerique which testified before the committee last May 5. That organization precisely stressed the point that it would perhaps be dangerous to give too much power to deputy ministers.
It is obvious that the commission always has more or less a veto on these various authorities, but I still want to point out that fact, because I think some wrongs might have been done in the past. In fact, I have in mind a case about which information was given to me by a civil servant. As in the case pointed out by the hon. member for Edmon-ton-Strathcona, those complaints did not come from the general public but rather from individuals who had been employed in the civil service. My information came from a person who was a federal civil servant during a period of ten years. I will not identify them, but that person was employed five years in one department and five years in another one.
Name that person.
I would not want to give the name, because that person is no longer with the government service. Still, it shows clearly that anomalies did exist at that time-
Another unproved statement.
-when our friends were in power-
Give us the name.

There is no need to give names in every instance and to lay charges as it is done now at the provincial level. I only want to point out anomalies to prove beyond doubt that there were injustices in particular under the former government and to show that now attempts are made to put the blame for all that on the Conservatives, who have been at the head of this country for only a few years.
Give us the name of that person.

And more particularly, in relation to the attitude of our opponents toward French Canadians or the bilingual employees. At that time, a suggestion was made to have French accepted as a communication language between offices located in the province of Quebec and those in Ottawa, or located in an area with sufficient French to warrant a bilingual staff. At that time this suggestion was not considered. On this point, I am happy

to find that section 47 of the new act referred to a moment ago by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm will do away with that anomaly. With your permission, Mr. Chairman, I am going to read this section into Hansard so that the opposition will be able to meditate on it, because I believe it will improve the situation which has prevailed until now:
The number of employees appointed to serve in any department or in any local office of a department who are qualified in the knowledge and use of the English or French langauge or both shall, in the opinion of the Commission, be sufficient to enable the department or local office to perform its functions adequately and to give effective service to the public.
I hope this clause will open a larger number of jobs to bilingual people. It has even been suggested during our discussion by a C.C.F. member that a course be given to present employees to enable them to acquire a better knowledge of both French and English. That was no doubt a good suggestion, but it is beside the point. The only thing that could be done to improve the situation would be to give French Canadians a better treatment, to give them their due share in the federal civil service.
Before I conclude my remarks allow me to quote from a book on Canadian dualism written by Mr. Mason Wade. This book was edited jointly in both languages by the University of Toronto and Laval University.

The interesting variant on the spoils system in modern administration that is implied in the quotation is no doubt an inevitable product of a bilingual situation such as ours. This is what Mr. Ward, the author, said. (Text):
But as the technical requirements of the service have grown, and as English Canadians staff most of the higher ranks, the senior departmental officers have not unnaturally sought more English Canadians to work with, and until after the second world war the proportion of French Canadians in the total service was dropping steadily. That is the end of my quotation, and I simply wish to draw the members' attention to the fact that this situation which prevailed in particular under the previous government was not improved at the time, as indicated by the author.
There is also the impression, which has spread among our population, that French speaking Canadians are not fit to fill positions in the federal civil service, or that they simply do not bother trying to get one. That will be said often, for instance, in the case of appointments made by the civil service commission to senior positions, following promotion competitions. In my opinion, that is not borne out by facts.

I have here an article in which it is said that very few French Canadian university graduates try to enter the government service. As pointed out in Mr. Ward's article, that is probably due to the fact that, when competitions are held for various positions, standards are used that fit the Anglo-Saxon mentality and which necessarily prevent those French Canadians who might wish to become federal civil servants to put forward their qualifications.
That anomaly has been stressed, in committee, by various bodies, namely the civil service association of Canada. A moment ago, a previous speaker-I think it was the hon. member for Ottawa East (Mr. Richard)-did refer to that. May I refer to page 7 of the submission of the civil service association of Canada, which reads as follows:
(Text):
We feel strongly that there should now he as much concern over patronage from within the ranks of the service as there was over political influence in 1918.
(Translation):
That fact was also stressed by Mr. Hughes, the new chairman of the civil service commission.
I refer here to an article which appeared on April 29, 1961 in the Ottawa Citizen, in which it is stated that there is still favouritism in the civil service. Perhaps that is just the reason. Perhaps that is the trouble, perhaps that is why the French Canadians do not have their fair share of jobs within the federal civil service.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to conclude my remarks by saying that confederation in my view, and this has often been said, is a pact between the two great races which founded this country. Many people, in fact, still consider the French Canadians not as equals but perhaps as inferiors or as the losers of a battle, and that is most unfortunate. But as long as this attitude will persist, we cannot consider ourselves as a great, united and independent nation where harmony prevails regardless of the religious or political opinions, or racial origins of its people, a nation where life is good, where western democratic freedom is intensely enjoyed every second, every minute, every hour, every day throughout the year, and for many years to come.
We were quoted as an example in the recent discussions between the French government and the Algerian rebels. I do hope those two countries will follow our example and will reach agreement.

People seem to forget, Mr. Chairman, that Canadians of French descent gave their lives for Canada's independence, more than a century and a half ago, when two attempts to take over our country were made, by our neighbours to the south.
Other French Canadians died on the field of honour to defend the freedom and interests of our common homeland, Canada, from the south African to the Korean war, making in the meantime an active and efficient contribution to the last two world wide conflicts.
I dare say that all those sacrifices have not been in vain and that the convention on which this confederation is laid is a pact under which certain rights are recognized to English and French Canadians alike, not only because the latter are to be tolerated, but because we have a full right to be here, and because we consider ourselves as equal partners.
On the other hand, if some persist in maintaining a hostile attitude towards French Canadians, always accusing them of being a vociferous, inferior and discontented lot while closing the door to higher posts before them by all sorts of intrigues which are humiliating for them, limiting their part to that of translator, it may be very unfortunate, but the confederation might get into difficulties, as recent happenings among certain groups in the province of Quebec would indicate. However, I sincerely hope that such turn will never take place, and I think that the new Civil Service Act will, on the contrary, help to improve conditions.
I shall probably have other remarks to make in committee on various clauses proposed in this bill.

Mr. Chairman, as I used to be a civil servant myself I have a special interest in this bill and I should like to take advantage of this opportunity to make a few observations on this clause. The civil service is a most essential part of the machinery of government. Governments may come and go, but the civil service ensures continuity in the administration of the affairs of our country.
The importance of this was impressed upon me most forcibly not long ago when I had an opportunity to visit France, for which opportunity I am greatly indebted to the Minister of Veterans Affairs. I was surprised, almost amazed at the extent of prosperity I found prevailing in France, and in particular 90205-6-503
1 Civil Service Act
at the outlook and attitude of the people. It is the attitude of a young country and one might say that the country has become rejuvenated. I made inquiries about this from responsible officials, having in mind the numerous changes of government which have taken place in France right up to recent years. I asked how this could possibly have been achieved. I was assured that in large measure it was due to the excellence of the civil service of France which, although governments had changed frequently, had provided the continuity essential for maintainnig development.
Mr. Chairman, may I ask the hon. gentleman what was the year of his visit? What year is he talking about?

I am talking about two weeks ago. I think about two years ago the estimates committee, of which I was a member, held some hearings into the civil service commission and a number of problems were brought to light. I presume this new act which is before us has taken care of most of those problems. At that time we found there were numerous categories of civil servants. There were permanent civil servants, temporary civil servants, casual civil servants and prevailing rates employees. There were alsc semi-civil servants, such as employees of the crown corporations, who were employees of the crown and were amenable to civil service regulations but nevertheless did not enjoy civil service status. One of the things that impressed me most was the fact that a civil servant could be temporary for as long as ten or 15 years. I was surprised to learn how many civil servants had been in that category for a very long time. I think one of the recommendations of the committee was that the number of temporary civil servants should be reduced. I have not had an opportunity to examine the bill since it was presented to the house a few minutes ago, but I do hope something has been done to meet that situation.
The civil service commission was set up as one of the safeguards of our freedom by ensuring integrity in the civil service and by eliminating undue political influence in connection with civil service appointments. The opportunities for patronage in the public service of Canada are now relegated to rather minor positions such as revenue postmaster, river guardian and a few minor, temporary jobs of that kind. I suppose that no matter how we set up our ideals we can never achieve them fully, but I was impressed by what was said by the hon. gentleman on my left who preceded me in this debate about patronage from inside the civil service. I do

Civil Service Act
not see how that could be taken care of by any type of legislation. I do, however, feel that we have not used the best methods of recruiting people for the civil service of Canada. Indeed, I have felt that some of the methods we employ perhaps defeat their own purpose.
Most hon. members receive copies of notices of civil service competitions requesting applications for certain vacant posts. On looking them over, one finds that the salaries offered are very often not in line with the qualifications and experience required or set forth in the notice. I have come across a number of cases where this has worked against the best interests of the public service of Canada. A very honest person will look at the requirements and say: well, I do not have those qualifications and therefore it is useless for me to apply for the position; and he does not apply. However, another person, perhaps not so modest, will decide to apply and it very often happens that the choice is finally made from a group of people who are not of as high a calibre as those who neglected to apply in the first place because they were discouraged by the high standard set out in the competition notice.
Then there is the matter of boards of selection. Unless the application form has been changed recently there is a space on it somewhere in which the candidate is expected to list all his previous jobs-the name of the employer, the length of employment and so forth. It seems to me that very often the more lines of employers a man can fill in on that form the better his chances are, because that is taken as being experience. Here again, I think the form is defeating its own purpose, because it is not how much experience a person has had that is important. The important thing is the kind of experience a person has had together with its quality. Very often this is not apparent from the application form.
Again, most competitions for jobs which carry an average salary require an applicant to come before the board of selection. I may say that I know something about this work because I used to serve on such a board before I became a member of parliament. I was a representative of the Canadian Legion on selection boards to make sure that veterans got a fair deal and that veterans' preference was preserved. I noticed two things during that short experience. One was that the questions asked by the person conducting the proceedings and by the government representative very often had no relation whatsoever to the job which was being offered. Often no real attempt was made to bring out information which was not apparent from reading the application

form. Often this resulted in the applicant being placed at a disadvantage because, naturally, he had been expecting to be asked questions about his knowledge of the job he was supposed to follow. It can be very disconcerting when a person is asked a lot of other questions which, to him, are not related at all to the job for which he is applying.
The other thing I noticed was that an opportunity obviously existed for whoever was representing the department concerned, to frame his questions so as to favour one candidate more than another. I think this is done more frequently than should be the case. In the final analysis this boils down to the integrity of the people serving on the board. If a person has made up his mind in advance, after reading application forms, that he wishes a certain person for a particular job it is not difficult for him to favour one applicant, or to frame questions to which one applicant can reply, and then to eliminate another applicant by asking questions which have no relevance or which that other person is not likely to be able to answer.
About a month ago a case arose in my own province where a number of applicants were before the selection board. They were kept waiting for a while and the very suspense of waiting for half an hour or an hour to be questioned is likely to be nerve wracking. It happened that one of the applicants at that time was under great stress because of some situation at home; his wife was ill, and there were other problems. When he went before the board he had a complete mental blackout. As a former teacher I can understand how that can happen because I have encountered the same thing when school children, who know what the answers are to certain questions, find their minds a total blank when they are called upon to give those answers on the spur of the moment. That is what happened to this person. He was a candidate for a job which he was qualified to do. As a matter of fact he had been doing it for a number of years to the satisfaction of his superiors. Yet, when he went before this board, because of the situation I have just outlined, he had this mental blackout and failed the competition.
I mention these things because I think great care should be taken by everyone who has the responsibility of sitting on these boards of selection. Then, again, since coming to parliament 12 years ago, I have encountered numerous cases of people in the civil service who have come to me and told me about their grievances. There may be some clash of personality, or the superior may like somebody else better. This person has been brought up and advanced ahead of

the person who has been on the job for a longer period and, according to the evaluation certificates, has done very good work. That, of course, is very upsetting to morale. I have known several people who have been on the verge of breakdown because they have been up against this sort of treatment. It is intangible. They do not know how to fight it. They feel they cannot fight it successfully anyway and so they exhaust themselves emotionally and nervously and come to the verge of a breakdown.
The other point that I should like to make has to do with remuneration. If we are to have the kind of civil service that we want for Canada we shall have to pay our top civil servants and all civil servants on the same basis as private enterprise pays its employees. There used to be a time when civil service salaries were much lower than those which prevailed in industry, and this was justified by what was supposed to be job security. I do not think that the job security argument was ever a good one because I think the person who is so much concerned about security that he would take a lower paying job is not the right type of person anyway.
As far as pensions are concerned, nearly all the big companies have their own pension plans and we are looking forward to the day when those pension plans will become portable. Therefore so far as pensions and security at retirement are concerned, the security argument had no foundation at all. However, as an employer I feel that the government of Canada should follow the principle of equal pay for equal work. This is not being done. It is causing a great deal of injustice. To prove my case I will cite what is happening on the Department of Transport vessels. The Department of Transport operates a number of icebreakers and lighthouse tenders and boats of various sorts. The captains and officers of those boats all have the same responsibilities and in many instances the boats are of practically the same size and are doing the same work; they are even doing it in the same waters; and yet because the crew of one ship is recruited in one province and the crew of another ship is recruited in another province there is a discrepancy in the salary paid to the officers and men on the different ships. I submit this is something that should not be tolerated; it is something that cannot be justified. The captains and crews are all carrying exactly the same responsibilities; they are doing exactly the same work; they are on ships of comparable size and they are not even confined to one particular water. They move back and forth in different waters.

Newfoundland icebreakers very often are employed in the gulf of St. Lawrence and vice versa. It seems to me there is no justification whatever for having one scale of salaries on one ship and a different scale on another. What I have said about the Department of Transport applies equally to boats operated by the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys.
There is also the question of pensions. We are still faced with the problem of many civil servants who retired long years ago when the dollar was worth much more than it is now and who did not receive a very big pension. I think we have some obligation here. I do not know whether it is taken care of under this legislation or under some special legislation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend realizes that it is not a matter for the Civil Service Act but for the Public Service Superannuation Act, an entirely different measure.

It may be under a different act but it is part of our responsibility toward the civil service of Canada and I do hope that something will be done about it.
There is one final point I should like to make before I sit down. I refer to morale in the civil service. I think we cannot place too much emphasis on the necessity for maintaining the highest possible morale in the public service of Canada. We have seen what has happened in many countries where subversion has entered in and people in sensitive posts have betrayed their countries and passed over vital information to the countries which are seeking to bring about our downfall. We may try to isolate what we call sensitive posts but that sort of thing is not confined to people in sensitive posts; it is a part of the general morale of the whole service. I think it is something that requires special consideration; it is something for which we are all responsible and it will in great part result from the type of people we select to administer this legislation and the way it is carried out.

Mr. Chairman, I have only one general theme to deal with at this timp and it is somewhat the same as I have dealt with in speeches during other sessions and by way of introduction of bills during other sessions. I refer to the question of bargaining rights. I made two or three different proposals which have met with some objection in the past. One was that the current Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act should apply to employees in the public service negotiating with their employer, with certain exceptions, such as the

Civil Service Act
right to strike, and that arbitration proceedings be employed instead of conciliation proceedings as they are known under the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. A variation of that this year was also proposed by myself by way of another public bill which in essence said that parliament would be the final arbiter of those matters and would in fact receive the report of the conciliation board under the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act and would make the final decision on any points which were contained in the report.
Other suggestions have been made and I would think the employees themselves who are concerned with this question of their right to negotiate particularly with their employer are not wedded to one particular system of bargaining as opposed to another. In essence I think what they want to have is the right of determination of their own destiny to the extent that that is possible by way of developing a collective agreement. They want the right to know who their employer is in the sense of whom they are bargaining with, and there is some doubt about that at the moment. Whom should they approach with respect to, first, the development of collective agreements or systems that exist governing wages, hours and working conditions and the like and, second, the processing of grievances?
I am quite sure that even the top officials in the various employee associations are not sure from time to time in their dealings on these matters whether they are dealing with the civil service commission, with the government or whether it is treasury board with whom they are dealing so far as having the final say is concerned or whether it is the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance with whom they should be dealing. Many of them are not sure from one day to the next, depending on the problem, who it is that has the final say with respect to the points that they want to discuss. There appears in that sense, as I said, to be no employer but some murky group of people who at different times have certain things to say about different matters.
As I have said earlier and also on other occasions, in industry employees are governed by the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act and an employee in industry knows who his employer is. When his organization or association or union sits down on his behalf either to bargain for a collective agreement or to process a grievance it is known who has the final determination. It may be true that in the preliminary stages or in all stages a union or association in private industry will deal with a lawyer representing a particular company or with

some employers' association representing a number of employers or possibly with industrial relations consultants. Apart from that, however, there is one person who is the employer. Behind the lawyers and employer associations there is a corporate structure. There is a general manager or a president and board of directors. There is somebody tangible with whom the employees can deal even though in an indirect way, and there is some difference between that system and that which exists within the public service so far as the relationships of the employees with their employer are concerned.
In private industry employees have the right to determine their own course collectively, to have some part collectively in the decision as to what will be their wages, hours of work and working conditions and how various grievances will be processed and dealt with conclusively. Whether or not the decisions are in favour of the employer or employee is immaterial to the point that there is some place where these differences of opinion can be determined.
This is not so in the public service of Canada or in the public service of a number of provinces. So far as the question of dealing with their employer is concerned, civil servants so-called-I do not care for that name but it is the one which is used regularly-employees in the public service of Canada are in fact, as I have said on many occasions, treated as second-class citizens. They are in a different class from other employees. They are in a different class even from employees of crown corporations who have the right of determination and the right of collective bargaining.
In addition to the suggestions I have mentioned, there have been other suggestions made so far as collective bargaining is concerned and some of these should be accepted by the government. I cast no reflections upon the committee that dealt with this matter but I think it is extremely unfortunate that the bill was introduced in the form it was in the first place, that it was reported back to committee of the whole from the standing committee in the form that it was and that there is no adequate or sensible provision for collective bargaining contained in the bill now before us. So long as there is no satisfactory system of collective bargaining there will continue to be difficulties. Employees of the public service are going to continue to have their wages depend upon the whims of a minister of finance and the manner in which he might be able to juggle the books. They are going to have to depend to a certain degree on governmental decisions, some of which may be made on a political basis depending on the relative nearness of

an election. They are going to have no formal, sensible approach so far as their dealings wth their employer are concerned, and this is going to continue to cause difficulties.
We passed a bill of rights last year which said in effect or was supposed to say that we believe in equality before the law, but the government does not believe in it when it comes to the public servants of Canada. I am paraphrasing the belief of the government in this regard because I do not think that anyone will say that the bill of rights has any effect or that it covers the activities of the government in its dealings with the public servants of this country. Yet this is the base from which we should start. These individuals should have the basic right that other people have to bargain collectively, to know who their employer is and to be able to deal with him in such a way as to bring about a conclusive result with respect to their grievances, requests and demands from time to time.
Inasmuch as we have a civil service commission that over many years has gathered a great deal of information, statistics and records about relationships of wages and so on in the civil service, it has been suggested that the commission should remain as it is with some alterations, that it should be the agency to which the various employee associations should present their proposals for a collective agreement or for changes and that the civil service commission would in effect be something akin to a conciliation board so far as private industry is concerned. It has been suggested that after the civil service commission had heard arguments from the employee associations and certainly after hearing the arguments from the point of view of the government representing the crown, which in essence I suppose is the employer, it would be in a position similar to that of a conciliation board and would make a public report and recommendations governing the provisions of a collective agreement. The public would have knowledge of this report in the same way as the public now has knowledge of conciliation board reports which are released by the Minister of Labour.
It is further suggested that if the terms of the recommendations were not acceptable to the government or to treasury board, whoever it is that happens to make the final determination, the civil service commission should then step out of the way. Suppose it is thought desirable to establish a negotiating committee of cabinet. This negotiating committee would then be able to meet with the representatives of the employee associations to bargain collectively upon the points at issue.
Civil Service Act
A few years ago we had some experience along this line in British Columbia when the provincial government said it was going to solve everything for the civil servants of that province by establishing a cabinet committee to meet with civil servants for purposes of negotiation. Everyone thought this was going to be a fine idea, but in one instance it took the British Columbia government employee association over 18 months to even get a meeting with the cabinet committee to talk about one grievance relating to a stationary engineer employed at the old folks' home. When I suggest a cabinet committee as the negotiating arm of the government, I am not suggesting that it follow the course established by Premier Bennett in British Columbia when his negotiating committee of cabinet took 18 months to even sit down with the representatives of the employees.
I think that the negotiating team of the cabinet or committee of the treasury board, whatever seems to be the desire of the government should be governed by some statutory requirement in connection with its meetings with civil servants, just as employers in private industry and unions must meet within a certain period of time if either side opens negotiations toward a collective agreement. I feel that there should be some time limit. In addition to that, I feel that if no agreement is reached at that stage there should be some form of arbitration to finally determine what the provisions of the collective agreement are going to be.
As I have said, a number of proposals have been made in this regard. These proposals have obviously been rejected by the government in office because it would obviously want to maintain the amount of control which now exists and retain the right to prevent public servants in Canada from having what should be their right, that is the right to be heard and the right to freedom of determination of their own affairs. It is obvious from the various refusals and arguments that have been made from the government side, that the government is not interested in extending, in a decent fashion, the right of collective bargaining to the public service of Canada. It is obvious that this government is not interested in even remembering the bill of rights, let alone extending it or making it apply to people to whom it should apply. It is quite obvious from all the comments that have been made that this government wants the Minister of Finance to be able, as he did about a year ago, to hand pick groups of people within the public service and say, you will get so much an hour more and you will get so much an hour more. This government wants

This is not good enough. The other day the hon. member for Greenwood upheld the Minister of Finance as being a truthful and honest person. No one disagreed with what he said at that time. Perhaps subsequent events made some alteration in his opinion, I do not know. The fact of the matter is that the Minister of Finance should not have-

The touchiness of hon. gentlemen opposite indicates very clearly that they do not want the public servants of Canada to be on the same plane and have the same rights, freedoms and responsibilities as everyone else has. They want to continue to treat the public servants as second-class citizens, to be able to juggle their wages, hours and working conditions as it is politically expedient so to do and keep them in a condition of subjugation. They want to continue to force them to be the cap-in-hand people who come to the cabinet or perhaps the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, with all her graciousness, and ask, please, madam, would it be possible to have a change in our working conditions?
I do not think that is good enough for the people in the public service of this country. As I said earlier, it is extremely regrettable that the government did not have the courage to bring in this sort of bill in the first place so that these people who have been treated as second-class citizens for many years by previous governments, could at long last be brought out of that condition and brought to realize that perhaps the bill of rights does mean something to them. The civil servants might be brought to realize that the bill of rights is not a fanciful group of words about which the Prime Minister likes to become emotional from time to time.

Mr. Chairman, on July 7, 1961, at page 7686 of Hansard, the Prime Minister gave a definition of the bill of rights as it applies to the civil service. This is one reason why I, as a member of the committee, am still worried about the lack of the right of arbitration in the bill that is now presented to the committee. Then, as far as civil servants are concerned, these words might be used, I think, to define their responsibility; one way to put it is that civil servants, like children, should be seen and not heard.
Actually, that is the one thing that is missing from the bill that is presented to us now.

Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member permit a question? Do I understand that when he used that phrase which he just used about civil servants being seen and not heard, he attributed that phrase to the Prime Minister; is that correct?
Yes.

Does he not know-he must know-that the Prime Minister quoted that as a phrase used by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. How can the member be so utterly unfair as to try to leave the impression again that those were the Prime Ministers' own words?
Actually, from what I read at page 7686, there is no indication that the Prime Minister was quoting anyone else. I shall read it for you, if you will listen.

May I ask the hon. member a question? Does he not know that those words were used by the Prime Minister as a quotation from the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate? Does he know that? That is the question.
