I rise on a point of order, Mr. Chairman. The hon. member for Russell has just said that the Prime Minister corrected that sentence after that interjection. May I say that the Prime Minister never corrected it. He had a clipping from a newspaper from which he quoted this statement by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.
I thought I was being quite bold in quoting the Prime Minister and I was not under the impression that he needed any help. As a matter of fact, I am sure he does not need any help to defend himself.
Not from the hon. member.

I accept the explanation of the Prime Minister and I tell the Prime Minister that actions speak much louder than words.

I personally think that in this bill presented to the house today there should have been included a clause that permits the civil service to go to arbitration. If it were possible for civil servants to go to arbitration it would eliminate many problems for them. There is no question that private industries and the leaders of private industries in Canada recognize collective bargaining. I wish to refer to a speech made by the president of Ford Motor Company of Canada, delivered before the British Columbia chamber of commerce on May 15, 1961, in which, with regard to collective bargaining, he said that he believes it is vital for business leaders to reaffirm their belief in the principle of collective bargaining as a device by which management, employees and union represented employees can represent divergent views in order to provide solutions with which both can live. Acceptance of this principle by management must be predicated, of course, he said, on collective bargaining rendering service to the whole economy.
The same thing exactly, Mr. Chairman, could apply to the employees of the civil service, namely that they be permitted to go to collective bargaining and that they be permitted to present their views in a manner that will be beneficial not only to the employees but to the economy of the country also. It would also prevent the government from procrastinating in making decisions in connection with salary adjustments, vacation adjustments or any other working condition that apply to civil servants. I know that the ministers or the hon. members across the floor will say that there is not procrastination. The last time an increase was granted to civil servants it was after demands that were about two years old. If they had collective bargaining or permission for collective bargaining, they would immediately apply to the board and prevent this procrastination that is a recognizable attribute of the present government.
There is another injustice that was done to civil servants at the end of a period of two years of procrastination. It was the fact that salary adjustments had been made to departments at different periods. It is my opinion and that of many of the people who sat on the committee that the adjustment in salaries should apply to all civil servants at the same time. If, because of an increased cost of living or because of other conditions, there is necessity to adjust salaries for civil servants, the necessity should apply to all civil servants at the same time, not to one department in January, another department in May and another one in November. All civil servants should be treated in exactly the same manner. There should

be no discrimination, as there is in some departments, in keeping them waiting longer for the adjustments they deserve and which have been agreed.
The hon. member for Edmonton-Strath-cona said that in his opinion civil servants were getting too much protection. Unfortunately I find that is the attitude of the government; they think civil servants are getting too much protection. Every time a minister or a member of the government speaks to an audience they talk of the efficiency and the quality of our civil service, and in the House of Commons they say these civil servants are getting too much protection.
I can advise the hon. member and the government that not only are civil servants not getting too much protection, but they are not getting the protection that is given employees in private industry. Civil servants are at the mercy of the government in respect of decisions that are made. For instance, while this may not be a very important example although the last statutory holiday was part of this bill, it was not granted to civil servants because the bill had not been passed in the house. I hope the necessary arrangements will be made so that the next statutory holiday will be given to civil servants and they will not be forced to lose it as they were last time.
There is another provision that should have been included in this bill but which has been omitted. While I think the bill is an improvement over the measure that was in force and had been in force for a great number of years, there are still many things which should have been inserted in the bill to make it more appropriate. Temporary civil servants should be entitled to the 2 per cent holiday pay as are employees in industry. This provision should apply not only to employees who work for a short period of time but also to employees who work for a number of days every week and are considered temporary employees.
The hon. member for St. Denis, as reported at page 4717 of Hansard, asked the Postmaster General whether it was true that temporary post office employees were asked to pass examinations. The Postmaster General answered-I can quote his answer if the committee wishes, but I do not think it is necessary-that temporary employees were asked to pass examinations because their salaries had been adjusted and they were receiving the same salary as clerks doing an equivalent job. He said their salaries had been raised from $1.26 to $1.72 an hour.
As reported at page 7183 of Hansard of June 28, the hon. member for St. Denis asked the Postmaster General whether temporary 90205-6-504
Civil Service Act
employees were going to be granted holiday pay. The Postmaster General said no, it did not apply to them. So the Postmaster General will not think I am misquoting him I will read his answer:
Mr. Speaker, I can understand the hon. member's preoccupation with holidays at this stage in our parliamentary session. I think many hon. members are preoccupied with the same consideration.
That was one of the humorous remarks that the Postmaster General usually makes perhaps to prevent a straight answer to a straight question. He continued:
In this particular case these people are working three or four hours a day. It is not full time employment. They are perfectly free to arrange for holidays if they wish.
In industry, whether or not an employee works only two or three days a week, he is entitled to 2 per cent of his salary as holiday pay and he is the man who decides when he is going to take a holiday. The fact that he is a temporary employee does not prevent him receiving that percentage of his pay for holidays. With respect to part time civil servants there seems to be no obligation under our present regulations to pay them for holiday time.
Industry in the province of Ontario pays 2 per cent of the salary to employees whether they are part time or full time. In this case employees are being asked to pass the same examinations as permanent employees if they are going to work two, three or four days a week regularly throughout the year, and it is my opinion that they should be entitled to 2 per cent of their salary as holiday pay. I deplore the fact that this provision was not included in the bill.
At that time the Postmaster General could not understand why these people should not take examinations and yet be treated differently from regular employees. I think the government should certainly have considered this question and included this provision in the bill presented to the house. If some of these provisions had been included in the bill I am sure our civil servants, who are recognized not only by the government but by the opposition as being the foremost civil servants in the world-this is agreed by everybody-would be a lot happier. I do not think it would cause any great headaches to the government and I think it would eliminate many of the problems that the civil servants of Canada have to face.

Mr. Chairman, in the discussion on clause 1 of this bill in committee of the whole house it is perhaps appropriate that I should make some preliminary remarks about the standing committee to which the bill was referred after second reading.

Civil Service Act
I wish to make it clear that for my part I felt the committee made remarkably objective study of the bill. I should like on my own behalf to express to other members of the committee my appreciation of their objectivity in trying to deal with what is of necessity a somewhat complex problem. The chairman of the committee conducted the hearings in a way that tried to take full account of the rights of all members of the committee and of all the associations which wished to be heard or make representations. I must say I found this a very pleasant relief from some experiences I have had in other committees this year and last year. But I am not going to discuss that aspect of the matter here. It was a very satisfactory experience to have that approach taken by the chairman and all hon. members from all parts of the house who were serving on the committee. I wish to express that thought at the very outset of my remarks. I think it should be expressed and I am quite happy to do so.
There is one interesting sidelight to the work of the committee. It seemed to me that the result of the rather lengthy and thorough studies given by the committee was to make us appreciate all the more the splendid work performed by those who drafted the original act in 1918. When one remembers that the act is now some 43 years old, the changed circumstances of the times, the changes in the civil service, the great growth in the civil service and the many new problems which have arisen, one cannot help but have an appreciation of how well the principles in the relationship of government-civil service matters were laid down in the old act. I for one am perfectly prepared to acknowledge that. I am happy to acknowledge it and to express appreciation to those who were concerned with the draftsmanship and sponsorship of the bill at that time.
It was a coalition government. I have expressed the thought previously on this bill that the original bill could probably not have been passed had it not been for the fact that there was a coalition government. It is rather interesting that the two people who were mainly concerned with the carriage of that bill later became judges in very high positions in the judicial system of this country. There is no doubt at all about the fact that it was the coalition government which passed that bill, and it was because it was a coalition government that it was possible to get so many clauses, strong clauses, I may perhaps call them, inserted in the bill. It was a very good thing. I, personally, take some pride in the fact that the two ministers who had so much to do with it were Liberals,

but the hon. member for Greenwood would probably say this was a mere accident.
Well, God moves in a mysterious way, his wonders to perform.

That is another pleasant debate which we shall leave for another occasion.
I wish to place some observations on record about the original act because I think it is proper to do so. The bill before us now does not change the basic concept of this original act at all, but it does make many improvements which the passage of time has shown to be desirable and necessary. The committee was able, because of the way in which it approached this problem, to have many amendments made in the committee. I think the bill which has come back to us from the special committee is very much improved as compared with the one that went to it. I have not a note of the number of amendments which were made in the committee but it was sufficient to warrant the reprinting of the bill. I think that is all to the credit of the committee. I think it indicates that people were willing to treat the subject objectively. For my part, while the amendments have not granted all I would have wished, they certainly are improvements and I am the first to acknowledge it.
There are many questions which I could raise. The hon. member for Inverness-Rich-mond, speaking earlier this afternoon, indicated that with the passage of this bill a new golden age would be ushered in for the civil service. I wish to point out that there is one flaw in that reasoning. Golden ages for the civil service, whatever is meant by that-and I presume the hon. member means good relations, high efficiency, high morale, and so on-will not result merely from legislation. They result from the treatment received at the hands of the government in office from time to time. Good legislation is a great help but it is not legislation which makes what the hon. member calls a golden age for the civil servants. That condition is brought about by a proper appreciation and understanding on the part of the government from day to day, whatever government might be in office, of the role of the civil service in carrying on the activities of government, an appreciation of the necessity of a strong administrative arm in any government if that government is to perform efficiently and well, and of the necessity of a strong and efficient civil service if the policies of the government are to be efficiently and well carried out from day to day.

That relationship is not easy to define in precise terms but it does require an understanding and appreciation which is not always given in an equal degree by governments. Indeed, if hon. members would look at the history of the civil service since the predecessor to this bill was passed in 1918 they will see that the low periods, the periods which were not in any sense a golden age of the civil service, were brought about not because of any change in the legislation at any point in that period of time but rather because of the changing attitudes of governments from time to time. The point I wish to make is, in other words, that not only must we have good legislation on the subject but we must have a good understanding of the problems of the civil service and a good working relationship and direction from the government, whatever government it may be. I must say I regretted part of the line taken by the hon. member for Joliette-L'As-somption-Montcalm and the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot. It seems to me both of them had lost their objectivity in dealing with what must remain a difficult and delicate subject, though a most important one in a country constituted in the way our country is. I think the problem they were seeking to deal with, the question of bilingualism in the civil service, was treated by the committee in its study as one requiring a great deal of attention, one of real importance. But it was treated as a question of bilingualism in this country because of the rights of the two languages and because of the historical origin of those rights and the need to preserve them fully in spirit as well as according to the letter of the law. Regrettably, the hon. mem-
Business of the House bers to whom I referred used the term "French Canadian" in this context. Indeed, one of them used the term "French Canadian" almost exclusively instead of using the term "bilingualism". Then they sought to digress into party warfare on the subject. As a matter of fact, the members who sat on the committee reached, I thought, a remarkable degree of unanimity on that point and on the necessity of trying to get the kind of legislation with regard to this aspect which would be satisfactory.
May I call it six o'clock?
Progress reported.
I wonder whether I might ask the leader of the house if he can indicate what business the government intends to put forward tomorrow and for the rest of the week?
Why not next week, too?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I did not anticipate that the opposition wanted to sit here for the rest of the week. I shall simply announce that tomorrow we shall carry on with what we are doing today. The order of business-if it is to be changed I will notify the opposition in good time-will be consideration of the Civil Service Act with which we have been dealing in committee, followed by interim supply. If it is possible to reach some solution to the problem of the divorce cases, we might have something to say with regard to that tomorrow.
